items.question: Was the research published in a credible venue?
items.rationale: The corpus metadata identifies an IEEE Aerospace Conference paper with a stable IEEE DOI; this is a credible conference-proceedings venue for aerospace systems work.
evidence: Corpus metadata DOI: 10.1109/aero.2014.6836317.
Paper title page lists a full conference-style paper with references and author affiliations.

items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The paper states multiple scope boundaries and modeling assumptions, including that the model is a prototype, not an accurate RAX satellite model, and that detailed modeling is limited to energy/data concerns.
evidence: Section 1: "It is not intended to be an accurate model of the RAX satellite."
Section 4: "Detailed modeling was minimized by excluding several other non-critical subsystems, such as attitude determination and control."
Section 4: "The proof of concept is limited to modeling energy collection and management as well as data collection and management."
Section 4: "All states were modeled in a binary fashion".

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The paper identifies the RAX 3U CubeSat mission, organizations, science purpose, operational scenario, ground stations, and the use of the model for design/trade-study and mission-simulation analysis.
evidence: Section 1: "RAX is a three unit CubeSat developed jointly by SRI International and the Michigan Exploration Laboratory (MXL) at the University of Michigan."
Section 1: "The purpose of the mission is to study the formation of magnetic fieldaligned electron density irregularities in the Earth's ionosphere".
Section 5: "The integrated RAX CubeSat model was used to analyze performance of different hardware and mission configurations."

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The model language, major diagrams, external analyses, COTS tools, bridge mechanisms, and system boundary are described in enough detail for comparison and partial replication, even though actual model files are not provided in the paper.
evidence: Abstract: "It is comprised of a SysML model created with MagicDraw, a set of analytical models developed in MATLAB, and a high fidelity space system simulation model created in STK. ModelCenter was used to integrate the analytical and simulation models."

Section 4: "Architecture of the CubeSat Mission is defined in SysML block definition diagrams shown in Figure 4 that includes the spacecraft, ground network, external environment experimental target, and control software".
Section 4: "MBSE Analyzer effectively allows SysML parametric diagrams to be executed by linking constraint blocks to executable ModelCenter models."

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Most outcomes are tied to the executable integrated SysML/ModelCenter/STK/MATLAB model, behavioral simulations, requirements diagrams, and trade-study workflow.
evidence: Section 5: "The integrated model demonstrates how to accomplish this by performing mission simulations using MBSE models."
Section 5: "These trade studies demonstrate the ability of the model and the tools to simulate an entire CubeSat mission."
Conclusion: "Results of mission simulations were used to check system requirements of minimum energy limit and data download."

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper provides executable case-study results, time histories, trade-study plots/tables, and requirement checks, but not flight validation or a non-MBSE baseline.
evidence: Section 5: "During a mission simulation, time history of the states of the satellite was collected."
Table 1 lists solar panel area, max battery capacity, orbital altitude, and ground station network trade studies with performance metrics.
Section 5: "Nonetheless, all three configurations satisfy the system requirement that \"the system shall download at least 1MB of data per day\"."

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: Requirements are represented in SysML and linked to value properties through satisfy relationships; simulations then evaluate these properties against requirements.
evidence: Section 4: "Satisfy relationships were used to relate requirements to system properties that are calculated via mission simulation."
Figure 6 caption: "RAX system requirements are verified by using the results of behavioral simulations."
Conclusion: "Results of mission simulations were used to check system requirements of minimum energy limit and data download."

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The toolchain and data-flow mechanisms are described, and future academic release is planned, but the paper does not provide a repository, released model, scripts, data files, or sufficient parameters for full reproduction.
evidence: Abstract: "The RAX CubeSat model will be made available to the academic community for further study and potential extension for more complex missions."
Conclusion: "We are planning to make available the RAX CubeSat model and associated manual to academic community."
Section 4: "Each integrated model was then imported into MagicDraw as a constraint block using MBSE Analyzer".

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: The study is a strong, credible CubeSat MBSE case with clear mission context, explicit integrated toolchain, executable simulation evidence, and requirements traceability. Its main quality limitation is reproducibility: model release was planned rather than demonstrated, and no full code/data/model package or external validation is reported.

bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Core tier retained: the full text directly addresses CubeSat MBSE, executable mission simulation, energy/power modeling, trade studies, and model-based requirements verification.
bibliographic_review_management.citation: Kaslow, D., Soremekun, G., Kim, H., and Spangelo, S. (2014). Integrated Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Applied to the Simulation of a CubeSat Mission. 2014 IEEE Aerospace Conference. https://doi.org/10.1109/aero.2014.6836317
bibliographic_review_management.title: Integrated Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Applied to the Simulation of a CubeSat Mission

RQ1.rationale: The paper substantially describes how a CubeSat mission and power/energy/data behavior can be modeled with SysML architecture, requirements, parametrics, activity diagrams, state machines, and external STK/MATLAB analyses, while simplifying non-critical subsystems and binary states.

RQ2.rationale: It claims and demonstrates integrability, trade-study support, consistency, and future reuse/reproducibility, but does not provide explicit reliability metrics or strong evidence for reproducible reuse.

RQ3.rationale: It integrates model-based verification of battery/energy and data-download requirements via executable behavioral simulations, but the work is a prototype based on an existing mission and does not report physical EPS pre-development test integration.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The study builds on the INCOSE SSWG FireSat work and Phase I/II CubeSat/RAX papers, then reports a Phase III RAX model developed from scratch based on the published CubeSat reference model. Potential overlap with references [7] and [8] is acknowledged in the paper; this extraction uses only the present paper's content.

study_context_population.mission_platform: Radio Aurora Explorer (RAX) CubeSat mission
study_context_population.size_form_factor: Three-unit CubeSat; the paper also describes CubeSats as one to three standardized 10 cm units weighing less than one kilogram each.
study_context_population.mission_domain: Space weather and ionospheric science; receiving and processing scattered radar signals to study magnetic field-aligned electron density irregularities.
study_context_population.organization_type: INCOSE Space Systems Working Group challenge project with industry tool vendors and an academic/NSF CubeSat mission context; RAX was developed by SRI International and the University of Michigan's Michigan Exploration Laboratory.
study_context_population.project_maturity: Phase III executable proof-of-concept/trade-study model of a realistic mission; the RAX spacecraft itself was real, but the paper states the model is not intended to be an accurate model of the RAX satellite.
study_context_population.lifecycle_stage_addressed: Conceptual/design-phase architecture, analysis, requirements verification, mission operations scenario simulation, and trade studies; MBSE is described as spanning conceptual design through operations, but the case focuses on digital simulation and design trades.
study_context_population.development_context: INCOSE SSWG CubeSat project initiated in 2011; a new nonproprietary RAX CubeSat model was developed from scratch using the published CubeSat reference model to demonstrate executable MBSE and trade studies.
study_context_population.model_maturity: Executable integrated SysML/ModelCenter/STK/MATLAB prototype with time-history and trade-study outputs; no flight-data validation, released model package, or hardware integration is reported.

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Small satellites are increasingly complex, resource-limited, coupled, and operate in dynamic environments; the study aims to demonstrate the power, scalability, and utility of MBSE tools and methods for CubeSat mission design and simulation.
modeling_scope: CubeSat mission architecture including spacecraft, ground network, external environment, experimental target, and control software
Vehicle subsystems including communication, power collection, power management, data management, payload, and bus
Energy collection/management and data collection/management proof of concept
Orbit, solar illumination, experiment, and download operational states
Requirements, parametric analyses, behavioral execution, and trade studies for solar panel area, battery capacity, orbit altitude, and ground station network
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: System-level CubeSat mission boundary with spacecraft, ground network, external environment, and operations/control elements; detailed subsystem modeling is applied mainly to power, communication, and data behavior while other functions are abstracted into bus or binary states.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: The paper excludes detailed modeling of non-critical subsystems such as attitude determination and control, groups less important energy/data dynamics into the Bus subsystem, does not use sequence or use-case diagrams in the RAX model, models states in binary form, and states that the prototype is not an accurate RAX satellite model.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: Some behavioral and numerical knowledge is required: orbit parameters, attitude/spin rate, solar incidence and panel properties, ground station locations/access and communication efficiency, power loads, battery limits, data buffer limits, and data generation/downlink rates. Detailed behavior of excluded subsystems is not required.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: The model uses a CubeSat reference architecture, simplified binary operational states, parameterized component properties, external STK/MATLAB analyses for behavior estimates, and aggregation of non-critical subsystems into Bus to enable useful mission-level simulation without detailed models of every subsystem.
model_artifacts_used: SysML requirements diagram with satisfy relationships
SysML parametric diagrams: GetStates, PowerCollection, UpdateEnergy, UpdateData, UpdateDownload
SysML activity diagrams: RunOperation, SendSignals, UpdateStates, Update State Values
SysML state machine diagram: CubeSatMission with orbit, solar, experiment, and download regions
generality_reuse_mechanism: Published CubeSat reference model used as a starting point
Parameterized SysML blocks and value properties for component and mission variables
External analysis constraint blocks imported from ModelCenter
Nonproprietary RAX model intended for academic community release
COTS tool integration pattern reusable for other CubeSat mission studies

implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The approach integrates SysML architecture/behavior/requirements with external analytical and high-fidelity simulation tools through ModelCenter and MBSE Analyzer, producing executable digital mission simulations rather than a standalone descriptive model.
tailoring_rationale: CubeSats have limited resources and coupled subsystems, making energy/data/communication interactions critical.
The proof of concept focuses on critical power and data functions and abstracts non-critical subsystems to reduce modeling burden.
The model follows a CubeSat reference architecture and uses COTS tools familiar to the small satellite community.
A nonproprietary model was selected to enable academic reuse and extension.

toolchain_interoperability_lifecycle_con.toolchain_architecture_data_flow: SysML in MagicDraw defines mission architecture, requirements, parametrics, activities, and state machines. STK, MATLAB, and Java analyses are wrapped in ModelCenter workflows. MBSE Analyzer imports these workflows into MagicDraw as external-analysis constraint blocks and executes them from SysML parametric diagrams. Cameo Simulation Toolkit steps through activity/state behavior, calls MBSE Analyzer at each UpdateStates action, receives computed values, updates state/value properties, and collects time histories.
interoperability_mechanisms: MBSE Analyzer bridge between SysML tools and ModelCenter
ModelCenter integrated workflows and Analysis Server import
ExternalAnalysis constraint blocks in SysML parametric diagrams
Explicit mapping between SysML value properties and external analysis variables
Cameo Simulation Toolkit calls to executable parametric diagrams during activity simulation
toolchain_interoperability_lifecycle_con.syntax_semantic_continuity_evidence: The paper shows external ModelCenter models imported as SysML constraint blocks and mapped to properties such as orbit parameters, mass, time step, sun_state, energy_level, and downloadDataMB; requirements are linked to calculated value properties. The execution success is evidenced by time-history results, but no formal semantic round-trip verification is reported.

Power-budget/EPS-adjacent behavior is represented through power collection, power management, battery capacity, energy margin, and power-consumption calculations rather than detailed electronics design.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by simplifying operational states to binary values, grouping non-critical subsystems into Bus, and focusing on mission-level energy/data dynamics.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include integrated toolchain execution, cohesive/consistent information management, sensitivity analysis, requirements verification, design-trade support, and planned reuse.

Evidence is strongest for integrability and trade-study/verification value through simulations; reproducibility remains planned, and reliability is not explicitly measured or claimed as an EPS outcome.

Quantitative trade-study outputs include energy-limit violation for quarter solar panel sizing, battery spillover with reduced capacity, and downloaded-data differences across orbit and ground-station configurations.
RQ3: Requirements are represented in SysML and linked to calculated value properties via satisfy relationships, enabling model-based checks of energy and data requirements.
Pre-physical verification is digital: Cameo Simulation Toolkit executes behavior while MBSE Analyzer/ModelCenter call STK/MATLAB analyses at each time step.
No physical EPS test procedure, hardware integration, or flight validation is reported.

The approach here focuses on the requirements analysis and functional analysis parts of the systems engineering process.

This paper presents an eight-step MBSE approach for defining the behaviors of the CubeSats. The approach begins with a well-defined set of mission requirements and ends with a representation of the functional architecture captured as an activity hierarchy.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The eight steps, SysML artifacts, MagicDraw use, actors, system boundary, use cases, and activity hierarchy are described with examples.
evidence: This paper describes an eight-step approach for defining the behaviors of CubeSats that begins with mission requirements and ends with a functional architecture modeled as an activity hierarchy using the Object Management Group's (OMG) Systems Modeling Language (SysML).
In this example, the MagicDraw modeling tool developed by No Magic Inc. is used.
The system is the CubeSat enterprise that has the responsibility for collecting and distributing the mission data to the Chief Scientist who needs it.

RQ1: A generalized eight-step SysML/MBSE workflow models CubeSat mission behavior from mission requirements to use cases, scenarios, activities, and an activity hierarchy/functional architecture.
The approach uses generic Collect Mission Data and Distribute Mission Data requirements that teams can tailor to unique missions.

It handles behavior definition through top-down refinement rather than requiring a full detailed behavior model upfront, but it does not explicitly discuss minimal behavioral knowledge and does not address EPS.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include single-source-of-truth, enhanced communication, reduced development risk, improved quality, knowledge transfer, traceability, recursive reuse, and generalizability.

Verification of functional requirements is named as future work, not a demonstrated part of the method.

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Small satellites are resource-constrained and operationally coupled, while conventional CubeSat design and operations often rely on intuition, simplified trades, and ad hoc unverified simulator integration. The objective is to extend a SysML MBSE framework by executing realistic RAX operational scenarios with integrated analysis tools.

The paper observes that beginners did better when they knew the CubeSat mission or incorporated tools.

This reduces complexity but does not eliminate the need for mission and tool expertise.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: Repository/collaboration and requirements traceability are mentioned, but formal governance, deliverable linkage, review gates, and ROI evidence are absent.

RQ1: A general CubeSat mission can be represented with SysML BDD/IBD, state/activity, requirements, and parametric artifacts spanning mission, flight, ground, environment, and selected subsystem functions.
Logical/physical separation and subsystem decomposition allow power, communications, data handling, and operations to be modeled at a useful abstraction level without fully detailed hardware models.
Acausal SysML parametrics and modular reusable components allow the same model structure to answer different analysis questions, but prior mission, subsystem, and tool knowledge remains necessary.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include feasibility/performance/robustness assessment, requirements compliance checking, design-update communication, toolchain integration, model growth, multi-modeler collaboration, and future reuse.
Power-related outcomes include simulating energy collection, subsystem power consumption, onboard energy/data time histories, and violation metrics for operational scenarios.
Reliability and reproducibility are mostly prospective or tool-capability claims; integrability is demonstrated more directly than reliability or reproducibility.
RQ3: Power verification is integrated through SysML parametric models linked to STK and MATLAB in PHX ModelCenter, enabling scenario execution, parameter updates, trade studies, and compliance checks before implementation in principle.
Behavioral verification is supported through CST execution of state machines and activity diagrams for ground/flight interfaces, OBC command dispatch, and communications states.
The paper does not show an EPS-specific physical-development verification campaign or validated comparison to RAX operational power data.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Appropriate licenses and vendor support are required for the simulation tools.
Setting up wrappers and saving/reopening PHX ModelCenter and MagicDraw models can be time consuming and inefficient.
Debugging MATLAB code and STK scenarios after wrapping into PHX ModelCenter can be difficult.
Wrapping STK models as parametric constraints and executing them using ParaMagic is in prototype stage.
The simulations currently execute individually; future work should combine them, such as jointly analyzing and optimizing power and communications.
Constraint-based solving for dynamic behavior and comparison with real RAX operational data are future work.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No public SysML model, scripts, wrapper files, or data package is reported.
The paper is system-level and operations-focused; EPS hardware architecture and verification procedures are only partially represented through power budgets/energy dynamics.
Most claimed reliability, reproducibility, and ROI outcomes lack measured evidence or baseline comparison.
The RAX mission was already launched and operating, so pre-physical-development verification is primarily prospective rather than shown as historical use.
Requirements traceability is described conceptually but not documented with explicit requirement-to-analysis/test links.

RQ1: A general CubeSat mission can be modeled as a reusable SysML Reference Model plus Project Model covering stakeholders, lifecycle domains, external environments/constraints, mission enterprise, space/ground systems, logical/physical architectures, and SysML requirements/behavior/parametric/structure artifacts.

The approach starts with low-detail, generic logical architecture and stakeholder/requirements terminology, then allows mission-specific teams to customize, add, remove, or decompose SysML elements as behavioral knowledge and requirements mature.

EPS is not modeled as a dedicated EPS, but power is included through logical power subsystem components, prior solar-energy/power-consumption modeling, Update Energy/Power Collection parametrics, and energy-level trade studies.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include integration of discipline models/simulations, cohesive and consistent requirements/design/verification information, reuse through a reference model, mission assurance artifacts, and pre-physical trade studies.
Reliability is not directly claimed or measured for the reference model; mission assurance is asserted conceptually without reliability metrics.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The CubeSat form factor, target university/team context, mission enterprise, space/ground segments, and development flow from logical architecture to physical architecture and development are described.

The basic CubeSat unit is 10x10x10 centimeters with a mass of about 1.3 kilograms, and this cubic unit is referred to as 1U.
The CRM logical elements are a starting point for a mission-specific CubeSat logical architecture, followed by the physical architecture and the CubeSat development.

evidence: SSWG's application of MBSE is enabled by the following: 1) a modeling language - SysML, 2) an engineering methodology, and 3) a modeling tool set from No Magic, Inc.

RQ1: A general CubeSat mission can be modeled by instantiating a reusable SysML CRM covering domain, enterprise, external constraints, space/ground segments, subsystems, requirements, measures, use cases, and logical-to-physical architecture transitions.

The Power Subsystem is included only as a high-level spacecraft-bus subsystem with the function to generate, regulate, store, and distribute power; no EPS architecture, behavior, power budget, or component model is provided.
The approach does not minimize required knowledge to novice level; it assumes intermediate space-mission, MBSE, and SysML understanding plus subject-matter expert guidance.
RQ2: Claimed MBSE outcomes include reusable starting points, consistency/uniformity across future models, reduced systems-engineering burden, model-centered requirements/design, and integration with external models/tools.
The paper does not provide EPS-specific reliability, reproducibility, or integrability outcomes and provides no quantitative outcome evidence or baseline comparison.
Reproducibility is planned through CRM reuse, reference information, and OMG specification ambitions, but actual public model assets and repeated-use evidence are not reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated at the model level through validation/verification packages, requirements traceability, viewpoints, representative mission population, V&V scenarios, and possible executable mission modeling with COTS tools.
Verification methods are stated generically as inspection, analysis, demonstration, and test, and mission-specific teams are responsible for regulatory compliance verification.
No EPS-specific pre-physical verification procedures, power-subsystem test cases, or electrical integration checks are reported.

extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: EPS relevance is limited to a high-level Power Subsystem block and generic electrical requirements references; no EPS component, mode, load, battery, solar array, or power-budget model is extracted.

Toolchain reproducibility is limited because model files, repository, exchange format, licensing, and detailed No Magic implementation steps are not reported.
The method is not a minimal-knowledge pathway because it assumes intermediate MBSE/SysML and space-mission expertise plus SME support.
The paper describes planned V&V but not completed verification results for either the CRM or mission-specific models.

Limited early behavioral knowledge is handled indirectly through qualitative MOE/MOP/TPM specification elements, but quantitative analysis still requires empirical or analytical relationships.
The study is not EPS-specific; battery cycles and solar cell life are only power-adjacent MOP examples for service life.

implementation_pathway_tailoring.mapping_to_se_activities_lifecycle_gates: The paper maps the approach to NASA-style systems engineering activities: mission objectives and external drivers feed CONOPS and requirements; requirements flow to subsystem functional/performance requirements, components, interfaces, and tasks; integrated analyses support conceptual design trades, feasibility assessments, point designs, requirement verification, PLM/BOM creation, and operations planning.
implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The approach goes beyond a standalone SysML architecture by integrating simulation/analysis tools, cost estimation, PLM repositories, BOM generation, version management, and lifecycle model continuity.
tailoring_rationale: CubeSat missions typically have low cost, limited resources, low mass, low volume, and low power.
CubeSats use a high proportion of COTS hardware and software, changing cost and verification assumptions.
Small multidisciplinary student/engineer teams and volunteer labor make conventional labor-cost tracking difficult.
Requirements and architecture are often undefined and dynamic during CubeSat lifecycles.
Lack of development, integration/test, and operations standards makes detailed traditional cost models difficult.
A reusable toolkit/framework can accelerate out-of-the-box analysis for CubeSat teams.

RQ1: A general CubeSat mission can be modeled using a SysML architecture framework that starts with mission objectives/requirements and flows them to CONOPS, operating modes, components, interfaces, and tasks.

EPS is included at architecture/power-budget level through subsystem taxonomy, power collection/management models, solar panel area, battery capacity, and on-board energy state; detailed EPS behavior is not fully specified.
The framework handles limited early knowledge by using standard CubeSat building blocks, placeholders, and parametric/behavioral models added as the design matures.
RQ2: Reliability is claimed as an objective of top-down/bottom-up architecture and budget-overhead modeling, but no reliability metric or validation is provided.
Reproducibility/reuse is supported by a common SysML framework, RAX model/manual availability, and academic-community release, but with no stable archive or reuse metrics in the paper.
Integrability is the strongest outcome: the paper demonstrates/claims integration of SysML with simulation, analysis, cost, and PLM/BOM artifacts using named tools and SLIM connections.
RQ3: Verification is integrated before physical development through executable SysML-linked mission scenarios and trade studies that evaluate requirement satisfaction.
Power/EPS-adjacent verification includes battery capacity/margin and solar panel/battery sizing trades in the context of mission scenarios, but not detailed EPS hardware verification procedures.
Evidence is moderate for system-level simulation/trade verification and weak for EPS-specific procedural verification.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Earlier behavior modeling lacked the ability to time-step through a behavioral scenario to determine requirement satisfaction across the entire scenario.
SLIM comparison and synchronization of SysML and PLM structures are maturing and planned for the next iteration.
Ground-system functional flow transformation into SysML is current work.
CubeSat cost estimation is challenged by COTS components, volunteer labor, dynamic requirements, lack of standards, and inability to use traditional mass-based cost databases.
Some launch and operations cost information is unknown, proprietary, or not defined.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: The paper is broad and enterprise-focused; EPS details are mostly power-budget and battery/solar sizing rather than detailed EPS architecture or verification.
Many outcomes are asserted or summarized without numeric results, baselines, effect sizes, or independent validation.
Detailed model files, equations, tool versions, integration scripts, and archive links are not included in the paper.
Several technical demonstrations are attributed to prior or future work, limiting standalone reproducibility from this paper alone.
No physical integration, environmental test, flight, or operational evidence is reported for the modeled EPS or system.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: RAX is a three Unit (3U) CubeSat developed by the University of Michigan Exploration Lab (MXL) and SRI International.

MBSE is the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design analysis, optimization, verification, and validation. It begins in the conceptual design phase, continuing throughout development and into later life cycle phases including operations.

A CubeSat architecture framework [10], such as the one shown in Figure 9, can provide a traceability map for translating the mission objectives and mission requirements into basic building blocks of CubeSat system components, interfaces and tasks.

The EPS branch is divided into Generation (leading to Solar Cells, which branch into Body Mounted and Deployables, and Fuel Cells), Storage (leading to Batteries and Super Capacitors), and Distribution.

Power modeling was used to investigate the time history of on-board energy and data, and the quantity of downlinked data. The modeling incorporated MagicDraw, ModelCenter, Systems Tool Kit, and MATLAB.

This enabled requirements verification for mission scenarios and the ability to perform trades on parameters such as orbit latitude, ground network size and distribution, and solar panel and battery sizes.
Requirements were defined for data collection, storage, download and for battery capacity and margin.
Energy state trade studies varied the solar panel area and battery capacity. Data collection trade studies varied the orbital altitude and ground station network.
SLIM manages these fine-grained connections to various versions of the models and can sync data or generate/sync complete model structures.
Our RAX CubeSat model and its manual are being made available to the academic community.

synthesis_consistency.notes_for_consistency_with_lineage: Classify this study as a broad enterprise-modeling and lifecycle-continuity CubeSat MBSE paper. Do not over-code it as an EPS-specific detailed design paper; EPS evidence is mainly power-budget, battery/solar sizing, and system-level requirement verification. It overlaps with earlier RAX/INCOSE MBSE papers but adds cost modeling, PLM, framework management, and release concerns.
synthesis_consistency.extraction_confidence_reason: Full text was available and the paper directly describes the framework and toolchain, but many claims are qualitative, some implementation details are delegated to prior/future work, and EPS-specific evidence is limited.

RQ1: The paper supports general nanosatellite/PNSat modeling by framing PNSats as cyber-physical systems and using abstraction levels that link natural-language requirements, logical requirements, models, parametric simulations, and behavior simulations.
Modeling can begin with broad mission objectives and abstract mission concepts, deferring detailed subsystem/domain behavior to later domain-specific design; however, EPS is not modeled.
Generality is achieved through a SMAD-style mission design flow, SysML as a common language, and formal refinement between abstraction levels.
RQ2: Reliability/high confidence is claimed through formal specification, PVS theorem proving, consistency checking, and correct-by-construction design.
Integrability is claimed through early formal methods, virtual testing at refinement levels, and reduced ambiguity across multidisciplinary interfaces.

Reproducibility/reviewability is only weakly supported through claims about rigorous requirements for peer review and archival purposes; no EPS-specific reproducibility assets or evidence are reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated before physical development by translating requirements into higher-order logic, using PVS for type checking/proof obligations, checking consistency within abstraction levels, and enforcing traceability/refinement between levels.
The paper's verification demonstration uses a railway-crossing example, not EPS or a satellite subsystem, so it is only analogical support for EPS pre-physical verification.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Formal methods cannot fix incorrect assumptions made in design.
Formal methods are not a panacea and may be cost prohibitive outside suitable areas such as complex interfaces or high-quality subcomponents.
The implementation of the traceability check is future work.
Manual traceability data capture for large software projects can require extreme time and effort.
Constraining refinements may limit the design space.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No EPS elements, power architecture, power budget, battery, solar array, or regulator models are described.
No concrete PNSat/CubeSat case study, mission, orbit, payload, or flight/operational evidence is provided.
No quantitative reliability, integration, reproducibility, cost, schedule, or ROI metrics are reported.
No executable SysML/PVS artifacts, profiles, model repository, or transformation tooling are made available.
The worked example is a railway crossing, limiting direct applicability to nanosatellite/EPS verification.

RQ1: A CubeSat mission can be modeled generally through a SysML-compliant, platform-independent reference model covering stakeholders, requirements, behaviors, architecture, technical measures, and V&V.
The model handles limited mission-specific knowledge by providing generic, loosely defined subsystem packages and a library of elements that teams progressively populate and tailor.
EPS is not modeled in detail; the Power Subsystem appears only as a generic subsystem, with historical mention of power-usage behavior and solar/battery trade studies.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include quality enhancements, reuse economies, reduced development time, increased design quality, institutional knowledge transfer, common baseline comparison, and standards/reusable-library potential.
No explicit EPS reliability claim or measured reliability outcome is reported.

Evidence for reproducibility and integrability is mainly structural and qualitative: traceable model elements, conformance criteria, professional review, university use, and pending OMG specification activity.
RQ3: Verification and validation are integrated as model packages and activity elements with plans, procedures, execution notes, results, status, hyperlinks, and verifies/validates relationships.
Verification is linked to requirements and validation to mission objectives or technical measures, supporting pre-physical-development planning within the mission-specific model.
No EPS-specific verification activity, test procedure, executable check, integration test, or physical result is presented.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Feedback from university teams currently using the CSRM will be evaluated for inclusion in the model in order to provide a better quality product.

Lessons learned may identify value-added model elements not currently in the CSRM, portions of the model that do not function as intended, and new capabilities to increase usefulness and applicability.
Processes for dissemination and control of the CSRM after possible OMG specification approval, update maintenance, and available formats have yet to be worked out.
Efforts to assess expansion from CubeSats to a broader class of satellites are future work.
The CSRM is methodology-agnostic and teams may need to modify the containment tree if the five fundamental elements are inconsistent with their methodology.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No dedicated EPS model, EPS requirement set, power-mode model, EPS verification procedure, or EPS test evidence is provided.

items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The paper repeatedly states scope boundaries and simplifying assumptions for generality, orbit modeling, launch, cost, ground station contact, and case-study intent.
evidence: Since each space mission is unique, the model architecture introduced here cannot be completely generalized, however a baseline structure can be maintained with modifications of the inputs and requirements made for each use case.
It should be noted that it is beyond the scope of this work to demonstrate complete novel mission solutions, but is instead aiming to introduce a design approach.
Because of this the cost metric defined here is not intended as a final price estimate, but as a measure with which to compare the relative cost of different designs.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The mission context is explicitly CubeSat/LEO with two conceptual design case studies and stated design variables, objectives, and lifecycle stage.
evidence: Two mission cases are studied; the first is an Earth observation satellite and presents a trade-off between ground sample distance and revisit time over a ground target, given altitude as the decision variable.

The second is a satellite with a generic scientific payload and shows a more involved trade-off, between data return to a ground station and cost of the mission, given variations in the orbit altitude, inclination and ground station latitude.
Once an acceptable mission design is identified during the conceptual/early design phase using this approach, design parameters tend to be held fixed throughout the remaining design life-cycle.

items.rationale: The architecture, equations, MATLAB implementation style, optimizer, and case variables are described for comparison, but no executable model, detailed component database, or formal MBSE language artifacts are provided.
evidence: As such, sequential programming is used to model the various disciplines, within the Matlab $ ^{\textcircled{R}} $ environment.
A general multi-objective problem can be described as the problem of finding a vector of decision variables and optimizing objectives; the study employs a controlled elitist genetic algorithm.

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claims about speed, trade-space visibility, baseline designs, and non-intuitive solutions are tied to the model-based architecture, analytic relationships, and MOGA search process.
evidence: Using the model-based architecture described in this work has additional benefits over identifying the trends shown in Figure 4, as it defines a baseline system design for each point in the solution space.
This work presents a rapid, model-based approach to the inter-disciplinary design of a CubeSat mission, through exploitation of analytical relationships at the inter- and intra-mission levels.

Global multi-objective optimization, in the form of a controlled elitist genetic algorithm, is applied to the architecture and is shown to find a Pareto set of near-optimal solutions from an arbitrary, user defined design space.

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper provides illustrative case-study results and a runtime metric, but lacks independent validation, flight/test evidence, stakeholder evaluation, and a controlled baseline comparison for several claims.
evidence: These results were obtained in 10 minutes on a personal workstation with an Intel i7 quad-core 2.2GHz processor, with a GA population of 500 and solution convergence after 102 generations (i.e 51,000 iterations of the model architecture).
Results from two case studies are presented; in the first, optimal solutions from a trade-off between ground sample distance and revisit rate are shown, over a range of orbit altitude.
In the second, it was shown that non-intuitive, near optimal CubeSat mission design solutions could be identified for maximum data return rate and minimum mission life-cycle cost.

evidence: A set of inputs, which includes the mission requirements, feeds each of the mission disciplines, from which one or more performance metrics are produced.

The approach to space system design is summarized by the process described in Figure 2, whereby the most suitable CubeSat platform is selected based on compliance with mission requirements and minimum cost.
A penalty function is applied in this case to remove the solution from the Pareto set.

RQ1.rationale: The study provides a general mission-level CubeSat modeling architecture and includes power demand, battery sizing, and solar array sizing using analytic approximations; it does not develop a detailed reusable EPS behavioral model.

RQ2.rationale: The paper claims rapid trade-space exploration, mission robustness, inter-disciplinary integration, and discovery of non-intuitive near-optimal designs; reliability and reproducibility outcomes are not demonstrated, and EPS-specific outcome claims are limited.

RQ3.rationale: Pre-physical feasibility checks for power, volume, lifetime, de-orbit compliance, and constraint penalties are embedded in the design model, but no formal EPS verification procedure, test artifacts, or requirements traceability is reported.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper cites prior CubeSat MBSE work including RAX operational scenarios and INCOSE Space Systems Working Group CubeSat/enterprise modeling, but this extraction treats the study as an independent MATLAB-based mission trade-space architecture.

RQ1: A CubeSat mission can be modeled at conceptual level using a reusable baseline architecture of trajectory, space, launch, ground, and performance modules, tailored by mission requirements and inputs.
EPS-adjacent modeling is limited to analytical power budget, battery sizing, solar array sizing, and feasibility screening rather than detailed EPS behavior.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled through long-term averages, analytical approximations, OTS component data, conservative factors, and simplified assumptions.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include rapid trade-space exploration, Pareto-set generation, non-intuitive design insight, whole-mission cost/performance integration, and possible mission robustness.
Reliability, reproducibility, and integrability are not demonstrated as EPS-specific outcomes; reproducibility is limited by absence of released models/data and exact component database contents.
The strongest evidence is the case-study runtime and generated Pareto solutions; claims about robustness and missed point-design solutions are less directly evidenced.
RQ3: Pre-physical model checks include power, battery, solar array, volume, lifetime, and de-orbit feasibility calculations plus penalty functions for constraint violation.
The paper does not report formal EPS verification procedures, requirements traceability, test cases, model checking, or hardware integration/test results.
Case I is said to verify the model architecture, but this is architectural sanity checking rather than EPS verification.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Since each space mission is unique, the model architecture introduced here cannot be completely generalized, however a baseline structure can be maintained with modifications of the inputs and requirements made for each use case.
It should be noted that it is beyond the scope of this work to demonstrate complete novel mission solutions, but is instead aiming to introduce a design approach.
Depending on the level of fidelity and/or rigidity of the analysis, certain links between disciplines may be neglected.
The nature of heuristic approaches in terms of finding only near-optimal solutions is considered acceptable in this study.
Because of this the cost metric defined here is not intended as a final price estimate, but as a measure with which to compare the relative cost of different designs.
This approximation assumes no GS mask overlap, a constant orbit period over the lifetime and operation of the communication system every time a GS is in view.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No formal SysML, requirements, verification, or traceability artifacts are provided despite MBSE terminology.
No model/code availability, exact OTS component database, or reusable package is reported.
EPS modeling is a power-budget sizing abstraction, not detailed dynamic EPS behavior or fault/reliability analysis.
No hardware test, integration test, operational flight evidence, or stakeholder evaluation validates the approach.
Runtime and non-intuitive solution claims are based on illustrative case studies under simplifying assumptions rather than controlled comparisons.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This work presents an architecture that identifies trends between conflicting objectives (e.g. lifecycle cost and performance) and decision variables (e.g. orbit altitude and inclination) such that informed assessment can be made as to which design/s to take on for further analysis.
The models within the architecture exploit analytic methods where possible, in order avoid computationally expensive numerical propagation, and achieve rapid convergence.

Since each space mission is unique, the model architecture introduced here cannot be completely generalized, however a baseline structure can be maintained with modifications of the inputs and requirements made for each use case.
A set of inputs, which includes the mission requirements, feeds each of the mission disciplines, from which one or more performance metrics are produced.
The mass, volume, power and cost of the platform are calculated as a sum of these parameters for each sub-system.
The battery capacity calculated in equation (5) is the minimum required to satisfy the demands from the platform, so the battery device would be a discrete size available that exceeds this.
This result verifies the model architecture and shows its usefulness at conducting trade studies via a basic example.

These results were obtained in 10 minutes on a personal workstation with an Intel i7 quad-core 2.2GHz processor, with a GA population of 500 and solution convergence after 102 generations (i.e 51,000 iterations of the model architecture).
This work presents a rapid, model-based approach to the inter-disciplinary design of a CubeSat mission, through exploitation of analytical relationships at the inter- and intra-mission levels.

This allows rapid, long-term visibility assessments to be made in fractions of a second (as opposed to minutes that is considered acceptable using numerical approaches), enabling many thousands of analysis iterations of the mission design space in the time typically expected for just one.

RQ1: The CRM provides a general SysML template for CubeSat mission enterprises, space/ground segments, subsystems, requirements, use cases, and technical measures.
Generality is achieved by methodology-agnostic packages, loose subsystem definitions, representative components, table-based population, and OMG/XMI reuse mechanisms.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by starting from logical abstractions, selectable detail levels, and use-case narratives before detailed model elaboration.
EPS is not modeled specifically; relevance is limited to a Power Subsystem, previous power trade-study background, and planned power parametrics.
RQ2: Reliability improvement is a motivation rather than a measured outcome; the paper cites high CubeSat failure rates and intuition-based design but provides no CRM reliability data.
Reproducibility/reuse are claimed through the CRM template, OMG XMI specification path, reference information, and non-normative implementation guidance.
Integrability is planned through SysML compliance and XMI cross-tool exchange, but no completed no-impact import/export demonstration is reported.
Traceability, table-based consistency, and technical-measure analysis are the strongest model-linked outcome mechanisms, though evidence remains mostly artifact-level.
RQ3: Verification is integrated generically through requirement properties such as verify method and verified by, plus satisfy/verify relationships.
Technical measures tie verification activities to MOE/MOP/TPM assessment and parametric prediction, but no EPS-specific verification examples are shown.
The CRM itself has a validation strategy with expert review, alpha-tests, and future metrics; detailed alpha-test results are not included.
No hardware integration, physical EPS test, or flight/operational verification evidence is reported.

The next steps include: 1) adding parametrics for power, weight, and cost, 2) validation of the CRM, and 3) continue working with OMG on making the CRM an OMG specification.

Part of that effort will include demonstrating that the CRM can be exported from CSM as an XMI file and imported into another modeling tool, such as Sparx System's Enterprise Architect, with no impact to the CRM.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: When launch failures are factored out, the failure rate of university missions approaches 50% [2]. The design effort for university CubeSats has largely been based on intuition [3].
The CRM is intended for instruction and for designing and building a mission-specific CubeSat.

Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) is the formalized application of modeling to support system requirements, design, analysis, verification and validation activities beginning in the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout development and later life cycle phases.
The CRM is systems engineering methodology-agnostic.

RQ1: The CSRM models CubeSat missions through a reusable SysML-compliant logical space-ground architecture rather than a mission-specific physical design.
Generality is achieved by keeping stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, and requirements unpopulated until a mission team tailors the model.
Power availability, energy collection, and energy consumption appear only as trade-study factors, not as a detailed EPS model.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include completeness, economies of scale, reuse, component sharing, mission success, and a unifying environment for universities.
Reliability is not explicitly claimed or measured, and reproducibility/integrability outcomes are system-level rather than EPS-derived.
Evidence consists mainly of assertions, reported professional vetting, and references to prior demonstrations, without metrics or baseline comparison in this paper.
RQ3: The CSRM includes model elements and trace relationships for requirements, technical measures, validation activities, and verification activities before physical development.
The paper does not report an EPS-specific verification procedure, simulation, hardware-in-the-loop setup, integration test, or physical test result.
Mission-level V&V support for the extended Mission Engineering use case remains to be evaluated.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM is based on Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) principles, is System Modeling Language (SysML) compliant, is hosted in a graphical modeling tool, and is intended to foster completeness and economies of scale associated with reusability.
The CSRM provides a CubeSat logical space-ground architecture.
The logical components are abstractions of the physical components that perform the system functionality without imposing implementation constraints.
The CSRM is a repository for systems engineering artifacts. However, it is not pre-populated with specific stakeholders, technical measures, behaviors, and requirements.

The CSRM provides for defining and tracing requirements from stakeholders, to behaviors, with technical measures assigned to subsystems and components to be certified through validation and verification activities.
A mission-specific CubeSat team downloads the CSRM specification and files from OMG for import it into their own graphical modeling tool.
The trade studies are based on the modeling of collecting mission observations, storage, downlink, energy collection, and energy consumption.
extending it beyond that point to incorporate a dynamic, analytical capability to assess overall mission performance would be challenging and an area that would require much further research.

As stated previously and shown in Figure 1, the current CSRM provides support for verification and validation activities. The level to which that supports Mission Engineering activities would have to be evaluated.
Stage 3 will consist of carrying out and reporting on implementation evaluations. Updating the OMG CSRM specification and files requires OMG and INCOSE approval.

RQ1.rationale: The paper substantially addresses generic CubeSat mission modeling with a reusable CRM, but EPS appears only as a logical Power Subsystem block and the approach assumes intermediate domain/MBSE/SysML knowledge rather than minimal behavioral knowledge.

RQ2.rationale: It claims system-level reuse, productivity, flexibility, traceability, and reliability-requirement decomposition benefits, but not EPS-specific reliability, reproducibility, or integrability outcomes, and no outcome metrics are reported.

RQ3.rationale: The paper centers on pre-physical-development model V&V through viewpoints, requirements traces, representative missions, and mission-scenario modeling, but this is for the CubeSat system/reference model rather than EPS-specific verification.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper references prior INCOSE SSWG CubeSat MBSE work on behaviors, COTS simulation, trade studies, and CRM status. This extraction treats those only as author-reported lineage within the current paper and does not rely on prior papers.

implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The work is a SysML MBSE approach enhanced by tailoring ECSS/NASA project-management structures, lifecycle reviews, PBS/WBS/CBS governance, and academic-resource constraints; it is not yet an integrated digital-engineering environment because external analysis/simulation integration is future work.
tailoring_rationale: ECSS standards are considered over-specified for nanosatellite projects.
Academic nanosatellite projects are not typically customer-supplier relationships.
Functional requirements are mainly derived from mission objectives.
Budget is directly allocated to hardware acquisition and software development, so schedule and cost structures can be derived from the product tree.
Student personnel can change continuously, and Business Agreement Structure can be neglected.
Framework is intended for limited-resource teams wishing to start CubeSat/nanosatellite projects.

RQ1: A general academic nanosatellite model can be organized as SysML lifecycle/views and a PBS repository that starts with stakeholders, needs/goals/objectives, ConOps, top-level requirements, and functional breakdown.
EPS/power modeling is included at an early-design abstraction through 212 Power System requirements, Power System BDD components, power/data IBD interfaces, and bus activation behavior.

The approach reduces dependence on detailed prior behavior knowledge by giving first-time teams standards-derived process flows, package structures, and reusable requirement/product identifiers, but it does not prove minimal-knowledge usability empirically.
RQ2: The authors claim MBSE improves reliability, traceability, design consistency, communication, planning, management, development, and deliverable generation.
Reproducibility is supported conceptually by reusable packages and standards-derived structure, but no model repository/open assets are provided.
Integrability is supported by hardware/software BDDs and IBD data/power/service flows, but no integration test or flight evidence is reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated into the model through requirements tables/matrices with Satisfied By and Verified By columns.
The EPS-adjacent Power System satisfies mode-transition requirement 100.1.6, and the Bus System Activation state machine within the LEOP flow is given as the verification artifact.
The paper reports model-level verification linkage rather than executed simulations, verification coverage metrics, physical tests, or acceptance results.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The reported application is focused on the mission analysis phase and PBS development for MASAT1.
The authors state that executable SysML modeling is a future goal.
The next step is integration with external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK and development of a graphical user interface.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No downloadable model, full requirements database, scripts, or open-source repository are reported.
No quantitative reliability, cost, schedule, communication, or reproducibility metrics are reported.
No executable simulation results, model checks, power-budget analysis, EPS test results, integration evidence, or flight/operations data are reported.
Venue name is not visible in the markdown, though DOI and publisher context are provided.
The EPS treatment is illustrative within a broader nanosatellite MBSE framework rather than a complete EPS-focused MBSE method.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This paper aims to contribute to research efforts to improve the success of university nanosatellite missions using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to facilitate the initial project management and design phases.

The proposed model-based approach is the result of experience gained from the MASAT1 project, a Moroccan university nanosatellite, and it is based on an architectural framework that allows the system to be described via a set of views.

However, with our limited resources, we encountered great difficulty in getting the project off to a good start, as most of the documentation and articles available cover the technical aspects of a CubeSat mission [11] and few articles detail the preparation and early phase management of a university nanosatellite mission.

The aim of using MBSE for a nanosatellite project is to create a model framework or repository that can be used by university teams (with limited resources) wishing to design CubeSat or Nanosatellite projects.
We used No Magic MagicDraw modeler with SysML and Cameo Simulation toolkit plugin.

The standard project breakdown method we just described works quite efficiently in an industrial customer-supplier relationship. However, some specificities of nanosatellite projects in an academic context allow for simplifying this structure model, since they are not in a customer-supplier relationship.

MASAT1 is a nanosatellite project initiated at the University of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fez, Morocco to put in place the basic and indispensable technologies (hardware and software) necessary to build a resilient, ready-to-fly CubeSat system, with efficient power management and low-cost mission control ground station [21].
The system requirements for the MASAT1 mission are implemented in the MBSE model using the requirement diagrams and tables available in SysML.
These tables describe the requirements and their relationship to other SysML design elements to facilitate requirements traceability, satisfaction, and verification.
The "Satisfied By" column shows the model elements that fulfill the requirement. For example, the "Power System" subsystem must satisfy operational requirement 100.1.6.

The 'Verified By' column shows the specific test cases that determine how the system meets the requirement. For example, the "Bus System Activation" activity diagram (Fig. 23), which is part of the LEOP flow (Fig. 22), is used to verify operational requirement 100.1.6.
The SysML internal block diagrams (ibd) can be used to model connections between bdd internal components in terms of data, power, or service flow.

The LEOP flow activity diagram is also a way to "verify" functional or operational requirements, such as the Bus System Activation state machine (Fig. 23), which verifies operational requirements 100.1.6. that validate operational requirement 100.1.6.

To improve communication, planning, management, and development, we implemented this approach, replacing ad hoc procedures in the work organization with process flow and model based on the different views of the system architecture.
The next step of this work is to improve the viability and practicality of the product breakdown structure model by integrating external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK.

items.question: Was the research published in a credible venue?
items.rationale: The paper is presented as an IFIP International Conference on Product Lifecycle Management contribution with Springer Nature proceedings context.
evidence: To cite this version: "17th IFIP International Conference on Product Lifecycle Management (PLM), Jul 2020, Rapperswil, Switzerland. pp.593-603".
Front matter: "submitted to an IFIP conference proceedings or other IFIP publication by Springer Nature".

items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The authors explicitly bound the analysis to unidirectional conceptual-to-detailed design transfer and describe the analysis as an initial step with future extensions.
evidence: Section 3: "we only consider the transfer from conceptual design to detailed design".
Section 5: "The limited but revealing analysis is only a first step".
Section 5: "For future work, we see the extension to other product development and lifecycle phases".

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The lifecycle stage and illustrative CubeSat Earth-observation mission are clear, but the mission is simplified and lacks form factor, operational, project, and EPS details.
evidence: Section 4: "we chose a small satellite" and "observe the earth surface and transmit the recorded images to the ground".

Section 4/Fig. 3: "The satellite consists of a number of subsystems, namely an Optical Instrument, a Power System, a Structure, a Communications System, a Thermal Control System, and an Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS)."
Section 5: "unidirectional data flow from conceptual design to detailed design".

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The paper names OPM, CPM, STEP AP242, DSM, and SFA and shows illustrative artifacts, but it does not provide the full DSM rationale, source model files, or a procedural recipe sufficient for full replication.
evidence: Section 2.1: "OPM provides both graphical (Object-Process Diagram) and linguistic (Object-Process Language) representations".
Section 3: "In total, 23 entities have been chosen: 3 for the OPM model, 10 for the CPM model, and 10 for the STEP model."
Section 4: "a spreadsheet of all entity and attribute information was created in the STEP analyzer and viewer (SFA) tool".

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Data-flow, heritage, and integration claims are linked to an MBSE/PLM digital chain and entity mappings, but many value claims are expressed conceptually rather than demonstrated in project use.
evidence: Section 2: "A well-integrated chain between MBSE and PLM is essential to facilitate the data flow from the conceptual design to the detailed design."
Section 2: "Such a chain would allow a product design team to store the design heritage and keep track of how the systems architecture transforms through the design process."
Section 3: "we use DSM to map the core entities from conceptual to detail design. Doing this, we identify the overlaps and gaps in the digital engineering information exchange".

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper provides DSM mapping, appearance-frequency analysis, and STEP entity counts as analytical evidence for interoperability gaps, but no baseline comparison, stakeholder evaluation, executable simulation, integration test, or flight/operational evidence.
evidence: Section 3/Fig. 2: "The first category contains the physical and informational entities. The entities of this category are the most frequently appearing ones".
Section 3/Fig. 2: "We have not found any correspondence of this entity with other entities in Fig. 1."
Table 1: "Product/part" count 69, "Geometry" count 86229, and "Action"/"Process plan" count 0.

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: The central traceability is entity correspondence among OPM, CPM, and STEP artifacts, including a CPM specification relationship, but requirements, verification, validation, and lifecycle gates are not traced through the models.
evidence: Section 3: "The cells at the intersection of different rows and columns indicate that two entities are corresponding fully (denoted by F) or partially (denoted by P)."
Fig. 5 description: "Artifact: Thermal Control System," linked to "Specification: Thermal Control System Specification" via a "satisfies" relationship.
Section 4: "CPM does not allow the description of "states"".

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The paper reports standards and a STEP analyzer/viewer tool and includes counts, but it does not make the CubeSat models, STEP file, or DSM data package available.
evidence: Section 2.1: OPM is "standardized in ISO 19450".
Section 2.3: STEP aims "to exchange and interoperate product data".
Reference 18 lists "https://www.nist.gov/services-resources/software/step-file-analyzer-and-viewer".

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: Credible venue and clear scope support quality, and the OPM/CPM/STEP comparison gives useful analytical evidence. mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Address traceability early in CubeSat conceptual design, make parameter impacts and requirement fulfillment visible, and provide an open-source model-based power-subsystem example that can reduce design effort and support learning.
modeling_scope: CubeSat power subsystem requirements and assumptions
Power-subsystem structural decomposition
Nominal behavior through use case and sequence diagrams
Power-budget analysis using constraint blocks and parametric diagrams
Parameter-impact and requirement-constraint traceability through Java extraction from Papyrus .uml
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: Subsystem-level EPS boundary including power generation, power storage, power supply control, and bus; component and parameter-level abstractions support power-budget equations, but not full spacecraft modes or hardware implementation.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: Activity and state-machine diagrams are not used; only nominal behavior is shown; mission modes are not discussed; complete CubeSat modeling and direct in-model visualization after Java execution are future work.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: The approach assumes familiarity with SysML/Papyrus, CubeSat power-subsystem concepts, and power-budget equations, but uses CSRM concepts and standard diagrams to reduce the amount of bespoke behavioral modeling required.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: Behavioral modeling is kept to use case and sequence diagrams for nominal functions, while externally fixed values are captured as explicit assumptions; the authors state the method can be extended with complementary behavioral diagrams for mission modes.

practical_implementation_pathway.rationale: The paper provides artifact categories, modeling steps through sections, concrete coding rules, repository reference, and a worked Java traceability scenario, though not a full deployment playbook.

toolchain_fragmentation_interoperability.rationale: The Papyrus .uml to Java to traceability-table data flow is implemented and demonstrated; however, cross-tool semantic preservation beyond this prototype is not evaluated.

lightweight_resource_constrained_tailori.rationale: The authors emphasize open-source accessibility and deliberately limit diagrams to concise essentials for CubeSat power-subsystem analysis, but do not quantify resource needs or tailoring effort.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: Cost/time value and future KPI study are mentioned, and traceability outputs could support decisions, but formal governance, deliverables, review gates, and ROI evidence are absent.

newspace_agile_distributed_rapid_iterati.rationale: The introduction frames CubeSats in NewSpace and the Java table is said to support rapid scenario evaluation, but agile, distributed, or iterative organizational practices are not studied.

RQ1: The paper models a generic CubeSat EPS through requirements, structure, behavior, and analysis packages in Papyrus/SysML, using the CSRM lineage as a reusable starting point.
The behavioral burden is intentionally limited: use cases and one nominal sequence diagram are included, while AD/SMD and mission modes are excluded or left for extension.
Limited or externally fixed knowledge is handled through explicit assumptions that the Java workflow can identify and apply during power-budget analysis.
RQ2: Reproducibility is claimed through open-source Papyrus and repository publication; reuse is supported by the assumptions profile and proposed future standard component profiles.
Cost/time reduction, early error detection, learning, and rapid scenario evaluation are claimed, but only traceability/scenario evaluation has moderate case evidence.
Reliability is not measured directly; integrability is mainly represented as model/data integration and toolchain continuity rather than hardware or organizational integration evidence.
RQ3: Verification is integrated before physical development by encoding requirement constraints and power-budget equations in the SysML model and extracting them from the Papyrus .uml file.
The Java code evaluates user-changed parameters, applies assumptions, recalculates dependent values, and marks constraints as respected or not respected.
A worked EPS scenario demonstrates agreement between expected power-budget calculations and Java-generated outputs, but no physical integration or test campaign is reported.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Activity diagrams and state-machine diagrams were not used because they were not essential for the analysis.
Only nominal behavior is shown and mission modes are not discussed.
The Java code should be developed further for more complex SysML models, including a complete CubeSat model.
Future work should visualize changes directly in the model after code execution.
A quantitative benefit study of cost and time KPIs is future work.
Expansion of the model to other subsystems is in progress.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No named mission, stakeholder, payload context, or flight project is described.
No baseline comparison against document-centric design or manual calculation effort is provided.
No stakeholder/user study evaluates understandability, learning value, or adoption difficulty.
No hardware, software-in-the-loop, integration-test, environmental-test, or flight evidence is reported.
The Java parser appears fragile because it requires strict naming and constraint-language conventions.
Power-subsystem verification is limited to power-budget equations and simple constraints, not full EPS behavior or faults.

RQ1.rationale: The paper models a nanosatellite mission at system/preliminary-design level using requirements, constraints, simplified discipline parameters, dependency graphs, DSMs, and known-unknown assumptions; EPS is represented mainly through power-budget parameters rather than a full EPS behavioral model.

RQ2.rationale: It claims MBSE/Nanospace can improve reuse, traceability, consistency, communication, time/cost, and integrability/data continuity, but the claims are mostly system-level and conceptual rather than EPS-specific or empirically demonstrated.

RQ3.rationale: Pre-physical simulations and Nanospace requirement flags check power/DoD, data, link-budget, and reentry constraints; however, verification is not presented as a formal integrated EPS model-based verification procedure.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: No other papers or prior extractions were consulted. This extraction treats the study as part of the Nanospace/CREME CubeSat preliminary-design line, with MBSE integration still in an early research stage.

RQ1: A general CubeSat preliminary-design model can be built from simplified discipline inputs/outputs, requirements, constraints, dependency graphs, and DSMs, with EPS represented by power-budget parameters such as payload/platform power, eclipse duration, solar panels, batteries, and DoD.

The approach explicitly accommodates limited behavioral knowledge through known unknowns, margins, expert estimates, worst-case assumptions, and modular dependencies that can later add mission modes or omitted subsystems.
RQ2: Claimed MBSE/Nanospace outcomes include improved communication, information sharing, traceability, reuse, consistency, system understanding, time/cost reduction, and data continuity, but evidence is mostly conceptual and system-level.
Reproducibility/accessibility is supported by open-source Nanospace and AGPL scripts, but model and URL details are incomplete in the Markdown, limiting independent assessment.
RQ3: Pre-physical verification is demonstrated mainly through semi-automated scripts and Nanospace requirement flags: DoD, power generation, contact time, link budget, data rate, and reentry constraints are checked before hardware development.
The EPS-related verification is not a fully integrated SysML/EPS V&V procedure; it is a database/API-linked preliminary simulation and constraint-checking workflow.

The chosen case study is the "The White Compass (TWC) mission, a theoretical academic concept developed during the "Space Mission and Systems Design" course at Politecnico di Torino.
The TWC mission aims to deliver GNSS services across the Arctic region using a constellation of 12 small satellites in two high elliptical Molniya-like orbits
