quality_checklist.overall_rationale: Strong paper for an open-source CubeSat MBSE preliminary-design workflow with clear artifacts, limitations, and toolchain availability; evidence is mainly a theoretical case-study proof of concept, with limited formal traceability and no physical, operational, or comparative validation.

bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Retained as core because the full text directly addresses CubeSat MBSE preliminary design, reusable SysML/UML model formalization, open-source tool integration, and power/EPS-related model-based analyses.
bibliographic_review_management.citation: Luccisano, G.; Salas Cordero, S.; Gateau, T.; Viola, N. Open-Source Data Formalization through Model-Based Systems Engineering for Concurrent Preliminary Design of CubeSats. Aerospace 2024, 11, 702. https://doi.org/10.3390/aerospace11090702
bibliographic_review_management.title: Open-Source Data Formalization through Model-Based Systems Engineering for Concurrent Preliminary Design of CubeSats

RQ1.rationale: The article directly formalizes a reusable CubeSat SysML model and abstracts operating modes and subsystem data so preliminary design can proceed with limited detailed behavioral modeling.

RQ2.rationale: It provides explicit reproducibility and integrability claims for open-source SysML-to-simulation workflows and power-budget analyses, but reliability claims are mostly generic and not EPS-specific or empirically validated.

RQ3.rationale: It shows model-derived EPS requirements lists and pre-physical power/data budget simulations, but it does not define or trace formal EPS verification procedures to model artifacts.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper positions itself as extending NSS/open-source CubeSat preliminary-design work and MBSE challenge discussions cited in the paper; no other corpus papers or previous extractions were consulted.

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Address data fragmentation and poor continuity between CubeSat SysML models and preliminary-design simulations by making a reusable, open-source CubeSat model the central data source for design parameters, operating modes, and budgets.
modeling_scope: CubeSat system architecture and subsystem/component BDDs
UML stereotypes for SystemComp, SystemMain, Battery, SolarArray, Transmitter, Receiver, Orbit, PropagationLosses, GroundStation, and OperatingMode
Operating-mode generalization and activity-profile data
Requirements list extraction and dependency-graph generation
Parser/database bridge to NSS simulation tools for power and data budgets
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: Spacecraft/system-level preliminary-design model with selected subsystem/component data and mission-environment entities such as orbit and ground station; mostly structural/data abstraction rather than detailed behavioral dynamics.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: Excludes detailed treatment of non-nominal/EOP modes such as detumbling, calibration, and safe modes; detailed AOCS/propulsion behavior and formal physical test models are future work; NSS eccentricity limitations are acknowledged.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: Users need mission concept, nominal operating-mode activation criteria, and approximate subsystem power/mass/data/orbit/ground-station values; detailed component behavior is not required at early stages.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: The method abstracts behavior into generalized operating-mode attributes, standby/on/peak consumption states, default/priority rules, and computeMass/computeCons flags that allow system-level values when lower-level components are not yet specified.
model_artifacts_used: NSS-generated power and data budget plots/reports
generality_reuse_mechanism: Reusable stereotype definitions with standardized attributes and units
Generic operating-mode activation and priority schema
Parser reusable for Gaphor models compliant with the proposed stereotypes
Model data can be changed while retaining the same formalization
Open-source repository under GPLv3
Tool/language-agnostic concept, though current parser implementation is Gaphor-specific

implementation_steps_or_phases.step: Characterize design data in the CubeSat SysML model
implementation_steps_or_phases.inputs: Design parameters, operating-mode characterization, CubeSat architecture, requirements, modeling tool/methodology.
implementation_steps_or_phases.outputs: Stereotyped SysML model and model file containing architecture, OMs, requirements, and design parameters.
implementation_steps_or_phases.actors_roles: Systems engineer, discipline engineers, students/design team.
implementation_steps_or_phases.prerequisites: Modeling tool capable of SysML/UML diagrams and applying the proposed stereotypes; preliminary mission data available.
implementation_steps_or_phases.completion_criteria: Relevant spacecraft, orbit, ground-station, subsystem, EPS/power, communications, OM, and requirements data are represented with stereotypes.
implementation_steps_or_phases.handoffs: Model file handed to the parser for extraction.

implementation_steps_or_phases.step: Parse the model file and generate exchange artifacts
implementation_steps_or_phases.inputs: Model file, dedicated parser, known stereotype definitions, and model-file structure.
implementation_steps_or_phases.outputs: Software-readable database plus optional requirements list and dependency graph.

implementation_steps_or_phases.handoffs: Database handed to NSS or other simulation/analysis tools.

implementation_steps_or_phases.step: Run preliminary-design simulations and analyses
implementation_steps_or_phases.inputs: Database, NSS or other selected tools, analysis configuration, mission/OM data.

implementation_steps_or_phases.outputs: Updated model file/source of truth for the next PD iteration.

implementation_steps_or_phases.completion_criteria: Design changes are reflected in the model without manual intervention where supported.
implementation_steps_or_phases.handoffs: Updated model returns to CE/PD workflow.

practical_implementation_pathway.rationale: The paper gives a three-step formalization, stereotype definitions, parser workflow, and TWC case that generates power/data budgets.

toolchain_fragmentation_interoperability.rationale: Data fragmentation is the central problem; the SysML-stereotype-parser-database-NSS chain is demonstrated, though cross-tool interoperability remains limited by Gaphor-specific parsing.

lightweight_resource_constrained_tailori.rationale: The paper targets open-source, academic, and budget-constrained CubeSat design and early-stage incomplete architectures, but it does not quantify resource burden or compare lightweight alternatives.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: Budgets, reports, requirements lists, and dependency graphs are deliverables linked to the central model; ROI and formal governance are asserted or implied rather than measured.

newspace_agile_distributed_rapid_iterati.rationale: The article discusses CE, real-time collaboration, future real-time versioning/cloud storage, and dynamic updates, but gives no agile/distributed team implementation evidence.

RQ1: A general CubeSat model is built with SysML BDDs plus UML stereotypes that standardize subsystem, orbit, ground-station, communications, EPS/power, and operating-mode data.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by abstracting behavior into operating-mode activation criteria, priority/default flags, and coarse power states rather than detailed dynamic behavior.
SystemMain computeMass/computeCons flags let early-stage models use subsystem-level values when component detail is missing.
RQ2: Reproducibility is supported by open-source tooling and a public GPLv3 repository with code, data, and documentation.
Integrability is supported by a parser/database bridge between SysML model files and NSS analyses, demonstrated through TWC power/data budgets.
Reliability benefits are mostly general MBSE/open-source expectations; no EPS reliability improvement is empirically measured.
RQ3: Pre-physical analysis is integrated by extracting model data into NSS power/data budget simulations, including EPS-related battery and solar-array parameters.
EPS requirements can be exported from the SysML model, but verification methods, pass/fail criteria, and trace links are not modeled explicitly.
The paper supports verification-readiness through budgets and requirement visibility rather than formal EPS verification procedures.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The parser is modeling-tool-specific and tailored to Gaphor.
Model file formats are not fully interoperable across SysML tools.
Operating-mode generalization focuses on LEO missions and excludes EOP/off-nominal scenarios such as detumbling, calibration, and safe modes.
Generic framework may require customization for specialized missions.
NSS tool approximations are acknowledged, including ECC treated as null in the TWC simulation.

Future work includes broader parser compatibility, non-nominal OMs, more detailed AOCS/propulsion, delta-V/propellant budgets, comprehensive dependency graphs, parser output selection interfaces, and other database formats such as SQL.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: Evidence is limited to one theoretical academic mission case and no physical, operational, or flight validation is provided.
No baseline comparison quantifies time, cost, error, integration, or reliability improvements.
EPS modeling is mainly budget/requirements oriented and does not include detailed EPS behavior, fault modes, verification procedures, or hardware tests.
Requirement export is demonstrated, but requirement-to-design-to-verification traceability is not.
Open-source availability supports reproducibility, but no third-party reproduction or repeated reuse is reported.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: The proposed formalization positions the CubeSat SysML model as the central data source throughout the design process.

extracting all the necessary data for simulation and analysis activities becomes feasible, independently from the variety and number of blocks in the model.
The electrical power system shall provide and regulate sufficient power to all other subsystems' components in each mission phase
One significant limitation encountered, as anticipated, was the modeling-tool-specific nature of the parser.
The source codes and associated documentation are available in a public repository

items.rationale: The paper gives explicit scope boundaries for the reference model and notes limits of earlier hypothetical modeling and future work still needed.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: CubeSat form factor, example missions, enterprise context, lifecycle stages, and operations phases are all described.
evidence: A CubeSat is a type of miniature spacecraft with a form factor based on the standardized unit cube, which is 10-centimeters on a side, and it weighs approximately one kilogram per cube.
The reference model can support all life cycle stages for a CubeSat mission.
The model also supports all phases of operations: pre-launch integration and test, launch, early orbit checkout, and full mission operations.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The paper identifies SysML, OOSEM, No Magic tools, model-element types, and a logical CubeSat boundary, but it is an interim-status description without enough detailed model content or release instructions to replicate the model independently.
evidence: The project's application of MBSE uses the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) and graphical modeling tools from No Magic.
The CubeSat Reference Model will provide the logical architecture.
The CubeSat Reference Model is approaching a sufficient level of maturity to begin sharing with the rest of the MBSE community.

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claims about integration, propagation, documentation generation, reuse, checklists, and consistency are explicitly tied to the SysML/reference-model workflow.
evidence: At the core of MBSE is the development of the system model that helps integrate other discipline-specific engineering models and simulations.

a properly designed reference model can serve as a checklist to these teams and promote uniformity and consistency across future CubeSat models.

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?

RQ1.rationale: The paper substantially describes general CubeSat mission modeling via a reusable SysML logical reference model, but EPS/power modeling is only summarized from prior phases and not developed as the central contribution.

RQ2.rationale: It claims model-enabled integrability, reuse, uniformity, consistency, and reduced SE burden, but does not claim or evidence EPS-specific reliability or measured reproducibility outcomes.

RQ3.rationale: The paper mentions generic verification/validation support, Cal Poly testing requirements, and future model correctness verification, but does not integrate or evaluate EPS-specific verification procedures prior to physical development.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper explicitly summarizes the SSWG MBSE Challenge sequence from FireSat through RAX behavior modeling, RAX trade studies, enterprise modeling, and the current reference-model distribution phase; extraction treats those prior-phase results only as stated in this paper.

RQ1: A generic CubeSat mission can be represented as a SysML/OOSEM reference model with stakeholder needs, objectives, constraints, lifecycle phases, operations phases, domain/enterprise boundaries, and space/ground logical subsystem architectures.
The model handles early or incomplete mission-specific knowledge by providing reusable logical elements and a general decomposition that users tailor into mission-specific physical architectures.

The project's application of MBSE uses the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) and graphical modeling tools from No Magic.

RQ1: CubeSat missions are modeled through a Cyber-Physical operation-scenario abstraction implemented as a Capella SysML-based Class Diagram MAM.
A reusable abstract MAM covers equipment, orbit, solar panels, battery pack, mass memory, ground stations, ROIs, and predefined equipment operation functions.

Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by parameterized high-level operations such as AlwaysOn, OnGroundStation, TimedOp, and RoiOP, hiding ForPlan source-code and Julia scripting details from users.
RQ2: Claimed value centers on requirements verification, visual configuration, simulator usability, faster scenario iteration, integration of model artifacts with simulation, and stakeholder decision support.
Reliability is only indirectly motivated through avoiding issues/failures from skipped systems engineering; no reliability metric, fault analysis, or operational evidence is provided.
Reproducibility and integrability are partially supported by the Capella-to-Julia-to-ForPlan transformation, but no open assets or independent reuse evidence are reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated before physical implementation by generating ForPlan inputs from the MAM and simulating power/data operation scenarios in Phase-0/Pre-Phase A.
NCBR2 verification evidence includes battery charge and memory usage simulations used to infer stable power and data balances.
The final feasible scenario was reported as an input to on-board flight software development, but no physical EPS integration test is reported.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The current version of ForPlan considers four predefined Equipment Operation Functions.
Applying the workflow to other satellite simulators would require changing the MAM to fit new inputs and changing C2F to the new simulator configuration approach.
Future work is needed to model user-defined Equipment Operation Functions and automatically generate the corresponding ForPlan functions.
Capella Class Diagram supports only one metalevel, so the authors had to define well-formed constraints to make the models interpretable.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No public C2F source, MAM files, full NCBR2 parameter set, tool versions, or executable replication package are reported.
The EPS representation is limited to power-budget-relevant battery, solar, and equipment power parameters, not detailed EPS electrical architecture, control, fault behavior, or reliability modeling.
Requirements are checked through simulation outputs but are not modeled as formal requirement artifacts with explicit traceability links.
Claims about faster, more practical, and easier simulation use lack user studies, effort metrics, or baseline comparisons.
No hardware-in-the-loop, integration-test, operational, or flight validation data are reported.
The specific publication venue and publisher are not visible in the accessible markdown.

toolchain_fragmentation_interoperability.rationale: RMM links requirements, code, tests, and defects and a generic requirements-management tool is mentioned, but no toolchain integration, data exchange, or fragmentation issue is addressed.

lightweight_resource_constrained_tailori.rationale: The RMM is tailored for stakeholder comprehension, reduced shall statements, and eight-or-fewer columns, which is lightweight for CubeSat teams, but resource constraints are not empirically evaluated.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: The paper mentions scope, cost, testing time, and defect mapping, but does not connect models to formal deliverables, management decisions, reviews, or ROI evidence.

newspace_agile_distributed_rapid_iterati.rationale: The paper discusses multiple stakeholder roles and CubeSat cost/accessibility, but not agile, distributed development, rapid iteration, or NewSpace-specific delivery cadence.

RQ1: RML/RMM offers a general, high-level way to model CubeSat requirements using process flows and mappings among objectives, rules, requirements, code, and tests instead of detailed behavioral simulation.
The approach is suitable for limited behavioral knowledge because it emphasizes stakeholder-readable objective models and trace links, but it does not model EPS behavior or electrical architecture.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include improved requirement quality, easier elicitation/analysis, ambiguity/inconsistency detection, missing/unnecessary requirement identification, test coverage, defect linkage, reduced testing time, scope control, and cost control.
Reliability is only indirectly touched through quality/testability claims and an OBC NFR label; reproducibility and integrability outcomes from EPS modeling are not evidenced.
RQ3: Verification is integrated into the requirements model through RMM columns linking requirements to code, test case IDs, test descriptions, and pass/fail results.
The example applies to OBC/radio/camera functions and suggests defect mapping, but no EPS-specific pre-physical verification procedure is modeled.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Future work will verify and characterize the efficacy of the approach.
Future work will test the approach in an actual project and update it based on that experience.
The OBC software design document is described as an initial document.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No EPS elements, EPS requirements, or EPS verification model are provided.
The NDSAT case is an example concept rather than a reported operational or flight project.
No specific modeling/requirements tool, repository, model files, scripts, or exchange format are reported.
Claims about quality, cost, testing time, and defect reduction lack metrics, baselines, or independent validation.
Mission context and lifecycle gates are only lightly specified.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The mission, platform, payloads, organizations, launch profile, and architecture-development stage are described in detail.
evidence: The SeaLion CubeSat mission is a joint project between Old Dominion University (ODU), the United States Coast Guard Academy (USCGA), and the Air Force Institute of Technology (AFIT).
The end goal is to produce a 3U CubeSat consisting of three payloads for on-orbit validation.
The content presented in this article is based on the prior mission profile from the launch at WFF into VLEO.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The paper names the language, rationale, file/folder structure, artifact types, examples, and generation mechanisms sufficiently for comparison and partial replication.
evidence: M30ML was chosen for its lightweight human and machine-readable textual syntax, file-based model interchange support (for persisting models directly on the local filesystem), ability to generate both textual and graphical views, and relatively minimal overhead with modern doctools [29].
The SeaLion mission architecture is organized into two main folders of architecture and of components [13].
YAML files are automatically processed using templates language (e.g., Jinja2) via a build shell script.

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claims about ease of use, traceability, documentation generation, consistency, and change accommodation are tied to YAML/M30ML models, generated diagrams/tables, templates, and docs-as-code workflow.
evidence: These tools generate documents via its own code for easy presentation on a local file system without any proprietary software while keeping the model content format-agnostic.
Figure 20 is a UML diagram of mapping of user stories to data structures generated from the YAML file shown in Figure 19.
This means that any changes made to the SeaLion mission architecture model can immediately be used to generate new documents.

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper provides case-study artifacts, generated views, repository availability, and anecdotal training observations, but no measured baseline comparison, model checking, integration-test, or flight/operational evidence.
evidence: Multiple team members of the SeaLion mission have been able to quickly learn the methodology of using the docs-as-code approach within a short training session with an experienced member.
A conference proceeding manuscript presented in AIAA SciTech 2023 was created purely by a docs-as-code format [4].
Implementation of the overall mission architecture has been successful for the original mission profile.

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: Traceability is central and is implemented through derivedFrom fields linking references, stakeholder needs, user stories, and data structures, with generated UML mappings.
evidence: For the mission architecture shown in Figure 9, generally data structures are derived from user stories. Furthermore, user stories are subsequently derived from stakeholder needs with their respective references.
The derived from field is used to tie back the data structure to a user story YAML file should it be applicable.
Figure 16 is an excerpt of mapping of stakeholder needs to user stories.

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The paper reports a public repository, local plain-text YAML persistence, Git-compatible workflow, non-proprietary document generation, and model-to-document continuity mechanisms.
evidence: The SeaLion mission architecture and methodology is available in a publicly accessible repository.
Documents should be in plain text as to be compatible with modern distributed version control system (e.g., Git) and for ease of use;
Proprietary services are not required to generate documentation, modify documentation, or modify models.

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: Strong reporting of venue, CubeSat context, method/toolchain, traceability, and reproducible docs-as-code artifacts; evidence for outcomes is mainly artifact-based and anecdotal rather than quantified, tested, or operational.

implementation_pathway_tailoring.mapping_to_se_activities_lifecycle_gates: The approach applies the NASA systems engineering handbook to CubeSat mission design in a top-down process from mission concept to subsystem component and flight-software specifications, with models used for design, specification, analysis, verification, and validation; explicit lifecycle review gates are not reported.
implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The study uses MBSE artifacts as the source of truth and enhances them with docs-as-code practices, Git-compatible plain text, templates, and automated document/view generation rather than using a conventional monolithic MBSE tool alone.

M30ML has lightweight YAML syntax and minimal overhead with modern doctools.
Models should persist on a local filesystem and not require proprietary software or cloud services.

Formatting-agnostic model content reduces duplicate documentation work.

RQ1: A CubeSat mission can be modeled at a general, low-overhead level using M30ML/YAML files for references, stakeholder needs, user stories, and data structures, with derivedFrom links providing traceability.

The approach captures expected ground-operator behaviors and flight-software data structures without requiring executable subsystem behavior models, making it suitable for teams with limited training but not for detailed EPS behavior analysis.
Component/DOF extensions aim to generalize CubeSat component, interface, BOM, and assembly modeling, but they were still under development.
RQ2: Reliability/mission-success benefits are mostly aspirational and system-level, motivated by high university CubeSat failure rates; no flight or test evidence links the model to reliability outcomes.

Reproducibility is the strongest outcome: public repository, plain-text YAML, local filesystem persistence, no proprietary services, and generated documentation are clearly linked to the model/toolchain.
Integrability is addressed through traceability and planned N2/interface/assembly artifacts, but integration-test evidence is not provided.
RQ3: Verification and validation are represented generally through MBSE activities, user stories, and data structures such as Satellite Health Data Packet, but not as formal EPS verification procedures.

Battery health and temperature fields are modeled as satellite-health telemetry, providing EPS-adjacent information before operation, but no EPS simulation, model check, power-budget verification, or hardware test integration is reported.
Planned N2 charts could support pre-physical interface review, including electrical interfaces, but the paper treats this as future work rather than demonstrated EPS verification.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The implemented mission architecture reflected the prior mission parameters, not the newly changed mission profile.
The components folder was work in progress at publication.
Component data-structure use was still partly in contention.
Training material needed improvement because current guides were not step-by-step tutorials.
Communication with subsystem team members was necessary and unavailable contributors could delay architecture completion.
Legacy design decisions made before the architecture model had to be gathered and adapted.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No EPS-specific architecture, requirements set, behavioral model, power-budget model, or verification procedure is demonstrated.
No quantitative evidence, baseline comparison, integration-test result, model-checking result, simulation output, or flight/operational data supports the claimed reliability or efficiency outcomes.
The method lacks demonstrated executable semantics, limiting behavioral verification claims.
The public repository is reported but was not inspected under silo rules, so reproducibility is assessed only from the paper's description.
N2 chart generation and component/interface modeling are partly future work, not validated integration evidence.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: Through model-based systems engineering (MBSE), the SeaLion mission architecture team was able to create models, as opposed to documents, that serve as the authoritative source of truth for the conduction of system engineer activities [1].
These models were used to conduct activities such as design, specification, analysis, verification, and validation of the system.
The end goal is to produce a 3U CubeSat consisting of three payloads for on-orbit validation.
However, many of the SeaLion project team members are new to spacecraft development and systems engineering.

M30ML was chosen for its lightweight human and machine-readable textual syntax, file-based model interchange support (for persisting models directly on the local filesystem), ability to generate both textual and graphical views, and relatively minimal overhead with modern doctools [29].

For the mission architecture shown in Figure 9, generally data structures are derived from user stories. Furthermore, user stories are subsequently derived from stakeholder needs with their respective references.
As an example, the second user story desire is to "verify that satellite is operating nominally" [13].
As shown in Figure 19, the data structure, with YAML file named '1-SatelliteHealth.yaml' is for determining the satellite's health.
This means that any changes made to the SeaLion mission architecture model can immediately be used to generate new documents.
The SeaLion mission architecture and methodology is available in a publicly accessible repository.

Current guides are lists of definitions and format guides rather than a step-by-step tutorial on using the approach, which has caused confusion among members that attempted to learn the material by themselves.

The methodology presented herein has accomplished the ability to create individual elements of the architecture in an human readable code that is also easy to make revisions to and persists on a local file system.

synthesis_consistency.notes_for_consistency_with_lineage: Treat this as the 2023 Systems journal article and not the earlier AIAA proceeding. It is supporting evidence for lightweight CubeSat MBSE/docs-as-code and only EPS-adjacent for battery-health/electrical-interface mentions.
synthesis_consistency.extraction_confidence_reason: The full Markdown paper was read and contains detailed method, context, and artifact descriptions. Confidence is lower only for EPS-specific synthesis because the paper itself provides little EPS detail.

Minimal user MBSE knowledge is supported by faculty/SME predefinition of well-understood subsystems, reusable packages, documented design envelopes, and a mission payload template.
The PSAT1U model uses system/component hierarchies, BDDs, specifications, and relationships rather than detailed behavior or executable simulation.
RQ2: Claimed MBSE outcomes include reduced design/development time, easier design-space understanding, automatic change propagation, reuse, and lower MBSE expertise burden.
Integrability is supported conceptually by documented payload mass/volume/power envelopes and well-understood interfaces, but no integration-test results are reported.
Reliability is claimed for EPS hardware choices such as NiCd batteries and watchdog timers, but the paper does not demonstrate reliability as an MBSE-derived modeling outcome.
RQ3: The EPS model includes an as-designed power budget and margins in the subsystem specification, supporting pre-build design review.
Mission payloads can be checked conceptually against power and physical-envelope constraints before a mission-specific instance is finalized.
Formal verification procedures, requirements-to-test traceability, model checking, simulation, or hardware verification integration are not reported.

bibliographic_review_management.title: Applying Model-Based Systems Engineering on CubeSat Budget Calculating

RQ1.rationale: The paper models a generic CubeSat as OPM objects/processes with four subsystems including EPS and budget attributes, using minimal OPM constructs and OPL; however, it does not provide a general behavioral mission/EPS model.

RQ2.rationale: It claims reliability/compatibility, consistency, standardization, and automation benefits from MBSE-enabled budget screening, but these outcomes are system-level and asserted or demonstrated only via a budget example, not EPS-specific evidence.

RQ3.rationale: It integrates pre-physical verification as executable model calculations, thresholds, and accepted/error states, with EPS contributing power/mass/size inputs; it does not define EPS-specific V&V procedures or hardware tests.

RQ1: A generic CubeSat is modeled in OPM as a system with subsystems including EPS, OBC, TRXVU, and Antenna System, each represented mostly through mass, dimensional, and power attributes.
The paper supports minimal-knowledge modeling through OPM's small set of objects/processes/states, generated OPL, and budget formulas rather than detailed subsystem behavioral models.
EPS is included as a parameterized subsystem and input to system budgets, not as a detailed electrical power architecture or behavioral EPS model.
RQ2: Claimed MBSE outcomes include rapid screening for reliable/compatible component selection, process clarity, automation, consistency/synchronization, standardization, and stakeholder comprehensibility.

Evidence for outcomes is strongest for executable calculation/accept-reject demonstration and weak for reliability, reproducibility, integrability, and ROI because no measured outcomes or independent validation are provided.

RQ3: Verification is integrated into the model through executable budget calculations, threshold checks, Error outputs, and Component Selection state changes before physical build.
The demonstration uses real ISISPACE subsystem data and an altered-data failure case, providing moderate evidence for system-level budget verification.
The verification is not EPS-specific beyond EPS attribute participation in mass, volume, height, and power budgets; no EPS test procedures or hardware validation are reported.

RQ1: Nanosatellite/small-satellite missions can be modeled generically using ARCADIA levels from actors to components, with operations and architecture co-defined across OA, SA, LA, and PA.

Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by beginning with coarse subsystem parameters and low-fidelity simulations, then progressively adding mode transitions, subsystem behavior, and component constraints.
Mixed-resolution extraction lets simulations use detailed PA data where available and LA abstractions elsewhere, preserving system-level analysis during partial design maturation.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include traceability, reusability, fidelity, consistency, early validation, reduced integration costs, accessibility/reproducibility, reliability, agility, and integrability.
Reproducibility is supported by open-source tools and public models/code; reliability and cost/integration outcomes are mostly qualitative and lack baseline or operational evidence.
EPS-related outcome evidence is strongest for power-budget feasibility and early identification of energy bottlenecks, not for demonstrated flight reliability.
RQ3: Verification procedures are integrated through PVMT-enriched Capella artifacts, parser-generated simulation inputs, and simulations for design-space, performance/functional, operational-consistency, and requirement checks.

For EPS, the PA decomposes power generation, storage, regulation/control, and distribution into components and uses dynamic simulations to evaluate battery charge, eclipse behavior, and mode-dependent power demand.
The framework performs verification before physical implementation, while hardware-in-the-loop and digital-twin verification remain future work.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This paper presents the first version of the unified Modeling and Simulation (M&S) framework MOSAiC (Modeling and Simulation Architecture for integrated Complex systems), which connects MBSE with open source, multi-domain simulation environments
The architecture proposed here leverages ARCADIA-based models as authoritative sources, interfacing with simulation tools through standardized data exchanges and co-simulation strategies.
Simulation models are developed incrementally, starting with low-fidelity representations based on coarse overall parameters, such as general subsystem mass, volume, and power consumption.

For validation purposes, the MOSAiC framework was applied to the design and analysis of the FIRE-EYE mission, a multi-satellite constellation dedicated to real-time wildfire detection and monitoring in the Mediterranean region.
Three key simulation domains were interfaced with the MBSE model: (i) Orbital Analysis; (ii) Power Budget Simulation; (iii) Link Budget Evaluation.
Figures 12 and 13 illustrate this evolution using the Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS) as an example.
thus informing corrective actions early in the design process, before costly implementation steps were taken
All models and codes presented in this work are available in a public repository, under the GNU GPLv3 license

RQ1: SAPPhIRE causal elements provide a common structure for representing CubeSat subsystem behavior, structure, function/action, and inter-subsystem Inputs/States links at conceptual-design abstraction.

The EPS was represented as one subsystem using a requirements spreadsheet, orbital power-generation spreadsheet, solar-panel datasheet, and power-subsystem assembly, with no appropriate Physical Phenomena file.
OPAL's consistent GUI and short training suggest a lightweight system-level modeling approach for CubeSat conceptual design, but not a complete general EPS reference model.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes are mainly improved traceability, data finding, heterogeneous file integration, change propagation, cross-subsystem navigation, and low training burden.
Integrability is supported by a six-subsystem case and user-study ratings; reliability and reproducibility are not directly measured, and EPS-specific outcomes are limited to model inclusion.
RQ3: No EPS pre-physical verification procedure is integrated into the model.
The authors explicitly state OPAL cannot be used as an effective requirements verification tool in its current state.

implementation_pathway_tailoring.mapping_to_se_activities_lifecycle_gates: The workflow supports needs analysis, system budget production, preliminary feasibility assessment, power-subsystem pre-sizing, architecture trade-offs, and potential handover to phases A/B/C/D if a manufacturer/provider joins while maintaining file standards.
implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The paper frames the work in MBSE and concurrent engineering, but the implementation is a multi-tool digital-engineering workflow linking system description, mission scenario, power budgeting, data conversion, and executable power simulation rather than a single formal MBSE model/language.
tailoring_rationale: The mission is highly agile, making solar-panel and battery sizing difficult and requiring coupled electrical, thermal, communication, mechanical, and AOCS trade-offs.
A 48-hour worst-case illumination scenario is used to keep preliminary sizing tractable while remaining representative of the mission.
A non-regulated battery-follower bus and DET boost regulators without MPPT are selected for simplicity and low added value of MPPT in the case.
Standardized files allow each subsystem expert to use specialized tools while preserving integration.

RQ1: A nanosatellite mission can be represented as a common technical reference combining system/subsystem description, geometry, mission scenario, ephemeris, attitude, and system budgets.

The EPS/electrical architecture is modeled at preliminary level with a power-subsystem model, mode-based power profile, and ephemeris-derived energy flows rather than detailed behavioral models for every subsystem.
Generality is pursued through standardized files, plugins, and common database handoffs, but the paper does not define a reusable formal reference model.
RQ2: Claimed value centers on integrability/interoperability, adaptability, rapid change analysis, parallel trade-offs, and preliminary sizing.
Reliability-related value is indirect: SOC/DoD margins and survival/no-illumination simulation indicate energy margin, but no reliability metric or operational evidence is reported.
Reproducibility is limited: standard files and tool roles are described, but model files and complete schemas are not provided.
RQ3: Verification before physical development is implemented through Opalis energy-balance simulations driven by model-generated power profiles and energy-flow inputs.
Worst-case illumination and survival scenarios use SOC thresholds to assess feasibility and battery margin.
The paper does not report formal requirements verification, hardware-in-the-loop, integration tests, or flight validation.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The described process is for preliminary phases.
The use case is a single 16U nanosatellite mission concept evaluated for feasibility by CNES with LESIA.
The power-subsystem sizing scenario is reduced to a 48-hour worst-case illumination period considered representative of the whole mission.
Extension to phases A/B/C/D is conditional on adding a satellite manufacturer/provider and preserving the file standard.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: Venue and publisher are not reported in the paper markdown or supplied citation metadata.
No formal MBSE language, metamodel, requirements repository, or traceability matrix is reported.
No executable model files, data schemas, repositories, or open datasets are provided.
No baseline comparison, quantitative process-improvement metric, independent validation, integration test, or flight/operational evidence is reported.
Simulation conclusions depend on tool models and assumptions that are not independently validated in the paper.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: The objective of this paper is to describe the approach through the prism of an electrical architect, that contributes to needs analysis, realization of power budgets, system sizing and energetic simulations through a specific use case.

The selected use case to illustrate this paper is a 16U nanosatellite operating on low-earth orbit its mission being the 3D mapping of hot stars dynamic environment by using ultraviolet spectropolarimetry measurements from space for the first time.

The overall concurrent engineering approach consists in setting up a common technical reference (satellite description and mission), with the aim of producing system-level budgets (mass, power, centering/inertias, data, etc.) produced by the various subsystems experts/architects.
To define preliminary power budgets,
The model is defined in the Opalis software. It is a proprietary but open tool developed by CNES that allows performing power simulations.
The main added value of this process is that it allows to define an adaptable and interoperable model.

Flight dynamics experts from CNES thus extracted from the global observation plan provided by the LESIA the worst case scenarios in terms of sun illumination, reducing it to a period of 48h only that could be used to size the power subsystem and still be representative of the whole mission.

The ultimate goal of the simulation process is to refine the power subsystem definition and to size elements (in particular cells and accumulators assemblies for solar panels and battery) in order to reach an energy balance between generation, storage and usage.
enables to perform several analyses, trade-off studies comparisons and sizings in parallel by taking into account every constraint and design impact easily
the interoperability of the different tools and methods, made possible by the standardization of files format, is a real enabler for the concurrent engineering process

RQ1.rationale: The paper models a nanosatellite mission at a general system-architecture level using ADs, MAU/cost functions, and uncertainty analysis; EPS is included only as an electrical power architecture/power-budget decision, not as a detailed EPS behavioral model.

RQ2.rationale: It claims reliability/robustness, reuse/repeatability, and integration/collaboration benefits from MBSE, but these outcomes are system-level and only partly tied to EPS/power modeling.

RQ3.rationale: Development and verification plans are mentioned and the architecture model is checked via tradespace, Monte Carlo, and sensitivity analysis, but the paper does not describe EPS-specific verification procedures integrated into an EPS model before physical development.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: No previous extraction or related papers were consulted due to silo rules. This paper should be treated as a supporting system-level CubeSat MBSE/tradespace study with only power-budget/EPS-architecture relevance.

Configuration-control details and model ownership/versioning are not reported.

It mentions Development and Verification Plans and system validation against mission requirements, but does not show explicit review-board evidence or a requirement-to-test trace matrix.
governance_roi_project_decision_linkage.evaluation_criteria_model_quality_useful: Model usefulness is evaluated by utility, cost, Pareto efficiency, Monte Carlo uncertainty bars, 95% confidence analysis, +/-30% sensitivity analysis, ranking stability, and comparison against reference 6U CubeSat architectures.

practical_implementation_pathway.rationale: The paper gives a full early-design workflow from requirements and ADs through concept generation, MAU/cost modeling, tradespace analysis, Monte Carlo, sensitivity analysis, and Concept 10 selection, with case-study results.

toolchain_fragmentation_interoperability.rationale: It describes Valispace, Excel, GMAT, FLUKA, SPENVIS/IRENE, and centralized data intent, but no formal or demonstrated interoperability mechanism is provided.

lightweight_resource_constrained_tailori.rationale: The model is tailored to a 6U CubeSat with COTS, mass/volume/power/cost limits, propulsion transfer time, radiation/TID, and low-cost/short-schedule constraints; utility/cost and sensitivity results guide resource prioritization.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: The study maps requirements and design to ASI deliverables and uses a cost/risk model, but does not report actual ROI, governance metrics, or completed review outcomes.

newspace_agile_distributed_rapid_iterati.rationale: The paper emphasizes COTS, low cost, short schedule, real-time Valispace collaboration, and rapid design iteration via tradespace tools, but does not document an agile process or distributed-team iteration cadence.

RQ1: A 6U CubeSat mission can be modeled generally at architecture level by defining subsystem architectural decisions, combining options into mission concepts, and scoring them with normalized utility and cost variables.
EPS is represented minimally as AD1 with power-source options and P_avg performance; detailed EPS behavior, control logic, and electrical interfaces are not modeled.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled through performance proxies, COTS/reference data, weights, Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis, and sensitivity analysis.
RQ2: Reliability/robustness claims are linked to Monte Carlo and sensitivity evidence showing Concept 10 remains favorable under uncertainty.

Reproducibility/reuse claims are linked to a structured workflow, equations, Appendix data, and statements that the method can be retuned for future CubeSat missions, but no external reuse demonstration is provided.
Integrability claims are mainly prospective, tied to a planned Valispace IDM for real-time collaborative requirements/budget tracking; no implemented integration test evidence is reported.
EPS-specific outcome evidence is limited to the finding that AD1 power subsystem and AD3 propulsion dominate utility variation.
RQ3: No EPS-specific verification procedure is integrated into a detailed EPS model before physical development.

The closest pre-physical verification mechanisms are system-level architecture checks: tradespace/Pareto analysis, Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis, sensitivity analysis, and reference architecture benchmarking.
Development and Verification Plans are mentioned as future/strategic outputs but not elaborated for EPS.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The Valispace model to manage actual CubeSat data is under development and not the article purpose.
Tools are tailored to BOREALIS and need adaptation, weight reassignment, and possibly performance-parameter changes for other missions.
Weights are subjective and based on engineering judgment, although sensitivity analysis is used to test robustness.
The model is a decision-support tool, not a single source of truth for choosing the concept.
The radiation satellite geometry layout is significantly simplified at this stage and will be detailed as concurrent design proceeds.
A calculation chain for dose during the ascending manoeuvre is under development, so preliminary linear extrapolations are used.
The ten concepts are selected partly by engineering intuition rather than exhaustive enumeration of all combinations.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No formal MBSE language such as SysML is reported.
No open executable model, repository, Valispace workspace, or machine-readable data package is provided.
EPS treatment is limited to power-source architecture and power-performance proxies, not detailed EPS modeling or verification.
Outcome evidence is model-based and preliminary; no integration, environmental test, operational, or flight data validate the MBSE outcomes.
Requirement-to-model-to-verification traceability is described at process level but not demonstrated with a trace matrix or model artifact.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: Emphasis will be given to the model built for the tradeoff analysis, explaining how it was built and used and providing the reader with all the elements to possibly reuse it for another mission design of the same satellite class.

Regarding the design process, starting from the scientific objectives of the mission, the mission requirements and constraints have been identified to understand the possible choice on each satellite subsystem for the CubeSat configuration.
AD1 Electric Power System Body Mounted Solar Array(2×6U+2×3U) Large Deployable Solar Array Deployable Solar ArrayHigh-capacity Batteries
In the context of the BOREALIS mission, MBSE has been integral to aligning complex biological and engineering requirements within the constraints of a CubeSat platform.
It is worth mentioning that the model under development on Valispace to manage the actual CubeSat data is not the purpose of this article.
The model incorporates normalized data for each variable based on the performance of each subsystem in the reference mission concept [Annex A].
Monte Carlo simulations were performed with 1000 iterations, ensuring statistical significance in capturing the distribution of possible outcomes.
The analysis confirmed the dominance of AD1 (power subsystem) and AD3 (propulsion system) as the most impactful parameters across all concepts.
This case exemplifies how the MBSE approach can not only validate engineering intuition but also provides insights that can lead to better-informed design choices.

By integrating parametrized tradespace evaluation, Monte Carlo and sensitivity analysis into the system engineering process, this study demonstrated the effectiveness of a data-driven approach to guide the satellite configuration.

synthesis_consistency.notes_for_consistency_with_lineage: Treat as supporting evidence for MBSE-enabled nanosatellite architecture selection and power-budget/EPS-architecture trade studies, not as a core EPS behavioral modeling or EPS verification study. No lineage comparison was performed under the silo rules.
synthesis_consistency.extraction_confidence_reason: The full Markdown paper was read and the relevant MBSE, mission, EPS-architecture, and verification-related details are explicit. Confidence is lower only for EPS-specific synthesis because the paper itself provides limited EPS detail.

items.question: Was the research published in a credible venue?
items.rationale: The supplied corpus metadata gives a Springer-style chapter DOI and the paper is formatted as a scholarly chapter with abstract, keywords, and references, although the venue/book title is not visible in the markdown.
evidence: Paper front matter includes: "Abstract." and "Keywords: Model Based Systems Engineering·RFLP·Requirementsin-Loop·Product Life-cycle Management·Decision Support"

items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The authors state scope boundaries for the CubeSat case and discuss limitations around behavior modeling, domain-specific tools, closed PLM environments, and long-term degradation.
evidence: "We did not considered on launch segment since we have concentrated on the spacecraft part."
"Modelling the behavior of systems in logical architectures can be challenging, and although Dymola is a useful tool, many domain-specific tools are widely used in industries."
"The closed nature of PLM tools can make it difficult to integrate these domain-specific tools, leading to increased complexity and costs."

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The paper identifies a CubeSat spacecraft case, LEO/orbit/eclipse operational context, early/conceptual development, and the post-release stabilized simulation assumption.
evidence: "RFLP approach has been used in a case study of Cubesat where the aim is to study the power curves of the onboard battery and optimize the sequence of operations to make sure the batteries does replenish after eclipse."
"The scenario was built in which the Cubesat after releasing into designated orbit had already detumbled and stabilized."
"In this paper, we have proposed a method to implement MBSE using RFLP approach in PLM tool using a Cubesat case study, to keep requirements-in-loop during initial phase of product development."

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The method, tools, architecture domains, and CubeSat electrical-power boundary are described, but equations, parameter tables, complete model files, DOE settings, and exact interfaces are not reported, limiting replication.
evidence: "Dassault 3DExperience allows the implementation of RFLP approach."
"Functional and logical viewpoints are in SysML language and physical aspect of the product developments uses CAD-models."
"The RFLP approach is implemented using Dassault Systemes 3DExperience platform to simulate a single viewpoint of a Cubesat, focusing on the electrical power view."

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claims are tied to RFLP, requirements parameters, SysML/Dymola behavior models, PLM connections, DOE, and simulation comparison with requirements.
evidence: "It is done by verifying each requirement during each phase by assigning a numerical parameter to each requirement."
"The model compares its computational results against the numerical parameters of the specified requirements to determine if the current configuration satisfies the requirements."
"These connections enable the sharing of data and information between different domains, facilitating the analysis, validation, and verification of system requirements."

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper provides a single simulated CubeSat power case with voltage and SoC plots, but no baseline comparison, stakeholder evaluation, reusable model evidence, hardware integration, or flight/operational validation for broader process claims.
evidence: "The important information that is visually depicted is that after 300 minutes the battery has replenished to its initial value."
"Analysis of the SoC data in 6(b) reveals that the SoC of the battery remained above 90% for a period of 300 minutes, which indicates that the margin is well-suited to satisfy the SoC requirement."
"In conclusion, the implementation of the RFLP approach in Dassault Systemes 3DExperience tool has proven to be highly effective in ensuring requirements-in-loop during complex product development."

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: Requirements are represented as numerical parameters, linked through ENOVIA/CATIA/Dymola implementation functions, checked by simulation, and connected across modeling domains.
evidence: "Requirements structure is defined in ENOVIA environment and numerical parameters are appended to the requirements."
"The RFLP approach relies on the use of implementation functions to enable the flow of information between the requirements defined in ENOVIA and the Dymola model."
"Following a simulation, the parameters obtained are compared to the required parameters to determine if they meet the necessary requirements."

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The paper describes a commercial toolchain and data-flow mechanisms, but no model repository, open assets, precise parameter data, or complete interface specifications are provided; it also notes closed-tool interoperability issues.
evidence: "Functional and logical engineering application in CATIA environment is made to read the requirement parameters which it then uses in behavioral modelling in Dymola."
"These implementation functions act as the foundation for the seamless transfer of information between the two systems throughout the entire product development life cycle."
"The closed nature of PLM tools can make it difficult to integrate these domain-specific tools, leading to increased complexity and costs."

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: The study is a credible and relevant CubeSat MBSE/PLM case with explicit requirements-in-loop traceability and EPS power simulation evidence. Its main weaknesses are limited replicability detail, no shared models, and broad process/value claims that are supported mainly by one illustrative simulation rather than comparative or operational evidence.

bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Retained as supporting: the paper directly addresses CubeSat MBSE/RFLP requirements traceability and pre-physical EPS power verification, but the central contribution is an integrated PLM workflow rather than a broadly reusable nanosatellite EPS modeling framework.

RQ1: A CubeSat can be represented using RFLP viewpoints in PLM, with requirements, functional/logical SysML architectures, physical links, and Dymola behavior models at decreasing abstraction levels.
The paper does not demonstrate minimal-knowledge modeling; it requires numerical requirement parameters, subsystem behavior models, and mission-planning/eclipse data.
The reported system boundary is the spacecraft after release/detumbling/stabilization, focused on an electrical-power viewpoint.
RQ2: EPS simulation showed SoC above 90% over 300 minutes against a 60% threshold and indicated the battery replenished to its initial value in the scenario.

Claimed process outcomes include requirements traceability, design decision support, configuration exploration, and improved interoperability, but evidence is mostly qualitative or single-case simulation.
Reliability and reproducibility outcomes are not quantified; model availability is not reported and the authors note degradation and closed-tool integration concerns.
RQ3: Verification is integrated by attaching numerical parameters to requirements and comparing Dymola simulation outputs with those parameters.
DOE explores candidate battery/EPS configurations; configurations failing requirements are treated as infeasible before physical development.
The digital test includes LEO/eclipse and power-profile inputs and produces voltage, SoC, and power plots used to assess EPS compliance.

RQ1.rationale: The paper gives a general CubeSat preliminary-design modeling approach and includes EPS sheets and power-component database categories, but it does not focus on EPS behavior or explicitly analyze minimal prior behavioral knowledge.

RQ2.rationale: It claims system-level outcomes for speed, cost, transparency, consistency, integration, and reuse, with some comparator metrics, but reliability/reproducibility/integrability are not evaluated as EPS-specific outcomes.

RQ3.rationale: The paper states that early integration enables verification to begin earlier and describes central consistency checks, but it does not provide EPS-specific verification procedures or pre-hardware test integration.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper itself links this approach to STAR/SPACE4YOU work and reports use on BOSS, Geo-Profundo, and a cislunar inspector mission; no prior extraction, bibliography, or external source was consulted.

RQ1: General nanosatellite mission modeling is implemented as a phase 0/A concurrent workflow with standardized S3D spreadsheets, a central data repository, and CUTE-DB.
EPS is included as one S3D discipline and as multiple CUTE-DB power technology categories, but EPS behavior is not modeled in detail.
Limited early knowledge is handled by theory/formula sheets, typical values, user manuals, component property data, and shared assumptions rather than high-fidelity behavior models.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include faster feasibility analysis, lower estimated cost, lower mass, improved consistency, reduced manual effort/errors, better collaboration, and technology-realistic component selection.
Evidence is strongest for the BOSS one-case comparator metrics and weak for reliability, reproducibility, and integrability claims.
EPS-specific reliability or reproducibility outcomes are not reported; EPS relevance is via power components and budgets within system-level outcomes.
RQ3: Verification is discussed as an early benefit of model integration and as central-repository consistency checking.
The concrete mechanisms are common-input checks, sizing/budget validation, compatibility assessment, and figures-of-merit comparison before physical development.
No EPS-specific verification procedure, test case, hardware-in-the-loop, or requirements-to-verification traceability artifact is shown.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The shown comparison uses only four concurrent sessions and not post-study refinement.
The S3D Tool needs improvement and optimization.
The Optical Payload calculation sheet needs updating and integration into the central repository.
Spreadsheets for other payloads need to be developed.
A dedicated C&DH calculation sheet must be created.
Comet and Matlab System Composer are being explored for enhanced MBSE and later-phase suitability.
MySQL and other database solutions are being evaluated to improve database management.
Mission Analysis and Structure & Configuration sheets are not linked to S3D spreadsheets and require manual input from external tools.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No formal SysML or equivalent MBSE language/model is reported.
No public availability of S3D, CUTE-DB, user manual, or case model data is stated.
No explicit EPS requirements model, power-behavior model, or EPS verification/test artifacts are provided.
The traditional-method comparator lacks methodological detail and independent validation.
No measured reliability, reproducibility, model-quality, or stakeholder-collaboration metrics are reported.
Toolchain continuity relies partly on manual transfers from STK/SolidWorks and informal presentations.

This is model-integrated communications verification during Phase C-D, not EPS verification and not clearly prior to all physical development.

RQ1: The paper proposes a general SysML layered model for nanosatellite risk management, not for EPS behavior.
Limited behavioral knowledge is handled through qualitative risk descriptions, likelihood/severity scales, RPI, and color-coded risk views rather than detailed executable behavior.
The model boundary is system/subsystem architecture and management artifacts for RVSAT-1.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include better traceability, ease of access, improved risk overview, reduced document burden, modularity, and reuse potential.
Reliability is only indirectly related through risk/failure management; no reliability metrics or EPS-derived reliability outcomes are reported.
Reproducibility and integrability are weak: Papyrus/SysML are named and future MATLAB/Simulink interfacing is mentioned, but no model files or implemented interfaces are reported.
RQ3: No EPS-specific verification procedures are integrated into a model.

The paper claims the hyperlinked SysML structure supports validation and verification access and future tool interfacing, but gives no verification cases, simulations, or tests before physical development.

RQ1: A general CubeSat space-and-ground system can be modeled with a reusable SysML CSRM containing requirements, architecture, stakeholders, technical measures, use cases, and V&V packages.
The CSRM handles limited early mission knowledge by providing a tailorable sandbox: it is not mission-prepopulated, can be pruned/expanded, and supports requirements/technical-measure truncation.
EPS coverage is only adjacent: the architecture includes Power Subsystem/Power Components, solar array, battery, and power-property roll-up, but no detailed EPS behavioral model is presented.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include reuse/sharing of components, lifecycle continuity via a central MSM baseline, traceability, interoperability through XMI/web publication, and design insight from property roll-ups.
No EPS-specific reliability, reproducibility, or integrability outcome is demonstrated; no metrics, comparator, flight data, or completed mission-team evaluation is reported.
Reproducibility and integrability claims are conceptual and tied to the OMG/XMI/web distribution mechanisms and model package relationships.
RQ3: The model integrates verification through Verification Activity elements, verifies properties, verified-by properties, verify relationships, and links to plans/procedures/results/status documents or diagrams.
Validation is similarly represented through Validation Activity elements, validates/validated-by properties, and links to technical measures, mission objectives, and stakeholders.
The V&V approach is generic rather than EPS-specific and is represented conceptually before any reported physical integration or test evidence.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: CSRM is not pre-populated with mission-specific stakeholders, technical measures, use cases, and requirements.
Levels of abstraction for requirements, constraints, and logical design are suggestions and must be tailored to mission purpose.
Requirements and technical-measure hierarchies may be truncated when adequate specificity has been reached.
Mission teams are free to adopt different logical architectures and modify the CSRM.
CSRM validation requirements are initially judged by the development team and are best evaluated by several mission-specific CubeSat teams.
Power, weight, and cost parametrics have not been added because they are considered more appropriate for a physical model.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No EPS-specific architecture, behavior, requirements, or verification procedure is detailed beyond generic power subsystem/components and power properties.
No named modeling tool, model repository, license, or accessible URL is reported.
No quantitative evidence, baseline comparison, completed case study, integration/test result, or operational/flight data supports claimed outcomes.
No executable simulation or model checking is reported.
Interoperability is asserted through XMI/web publication but not validated by cross-tool exchange evidence.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: The CSRM is intended for use at the university level for designing and building a mission-specific CubeSat.

CubeSat, a type of nanosatellite, is a low-cost standardized satellite with its origin in the CubeSat Project which was established in 1999 by California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly), San Luis Obispo and Stanford University's Space and Systems Development Laboratory (SSDL).

Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) is the formalized application of modeling in support of all design activities (e.g. system requirements, design analysis, verification, and validation activities) beginning in the conceptual design phase and continuing throughout development and later life cycle phases including operations, maintenance, and retirement.
The CSRM provides the logical architecture of a CubeSat space and ground system.
The CSRM is a repository for systems engineering artifacts. However, it is not pre-populated with specific stakeholders, technical measures, use cases, and requirements.
the levels of abstraction in the CSRM for requirements, constraints and logical design are presented as suggestions and must be tailored to the mission purpose.

The CSRM logical components are intended to be reused as a starting point for a mission-specific CubeSat logical architecture followed by the development of physical architecture during CubeSat development.
The mission team downloads the CSRM from OMG to establish the initial instantiation of their MSM.
There is a trade-off between not enough detail and unnecessary detail.
The MSM is maintained throughout all phases of development and operations as the single and central design baseline.
The Verification Activity element describes the process for verifying an element, e.g. a requirement.
The verify relationship is a relationship between a requirement and a test case or other model element that is used to verify the requirement is satisfied.
The Validation Activity element has a validates property. The Technical Measure or Mission Objective element has a validated by property.
The Web Published CSRM allows a user to explore and evaluate the CSRM without the need to acquire a graphical modeling tool.
The Next Steps section of Reference [5] mentioned adding parametrics for power, weight, and cost. They have not been added since they are more appropriate for a physical model.

RQ1: A nanosatellite mission can be modeled from stakeholder needs through Arcadia operational, system, logical, and physical architecture layers in Capella.
EPS can be represented through requirements for continuous power, logical functions for generation/storage/distribution, and physical components such as solar panels, batteries, controllers, and PDU.
The method reduces dependence on early technology choices by defining logical functions before physical architecture, but it still requires mission modes, interface assumptions, and subsystem data.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include technical consistency, coherency, minimized errors, improved communication, traceability, easier integration, avoided rework, shorter preliminary design time, and a more reliable design.
Reliability and integrability claims are linked to unified modeling, traceability, early validation, and change governance, but are mostly qualitative rather than EPS-specific.
Reproducibility is supported by open-source Capella and detailed figures/tables, but limited by unavailable model assets and permission-controlled repository access.
RQ3: Verification procedures are represented through Capella requirement/test-case links, traceability matrices, requirement coverage diagrams, and validation criteria from component to system level.
EPS-related pre-physical verification is mainly power-budget analysis by mode, requirement allocation to EPS components, and cross-subsystem model consistency checks.
The paper reports orbital, thermal, communications/link-budget and power analyses before manufacturing, but no EPS hardware integration or flight validation.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Actual manufacturing of subsystems has not yet started.
Thermal analysis is preliminary and further detailed design analysis is crucial.
No comparative study against a traditional approach was conducted because of budget constraints and burden of parallel teams.
Comparison with the Spiral Model and other iterative approaches was beyond scope and left for future work.
Data availability statement says no new data were created or analyzed and data sharing is not applicable.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: EPS modeling is described in power-budget and architecture terms, but the paper is system-level and not primarily EPS MBSE verification research.
Claimed MBSE benefits lack defect metrics, rework counts, model-check reports, integration-test evidence, or flight/operational data.
Model artifacts are shown as figures but the underlying Capella model/repository is not openly available in the paper.
Interoperability between Capella and external analysis tools is process-based rather than described as an automated digital thread.
Reliability claims are qualitative and not quantified through reliability models or EPS dependability analysis.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This allowed the digitalization of the system, which was represented by models that contain requirements, architecture, and interfaces between the different parts of the system.

Capella, an open-source MBSE software (version 6.1), facilitated the transition from a traditional document-based approach to a dynamic model analysis and traceability of functionalities throughout the mission.

Requirements were established initially from mission concept, translated into Capella, and linked to various model elements, including operational scenarios, system functions, logical components, and physical designs.
From the component to system level, each part was linked to test cases and validation criteria, enabling systematic verification of compliance with mission objectives.
Traceability: the requirements for continuous power were linked to specific physical components, such as solar panels and batteries, ensuring direct alignment from requirement to implementation.
The power budget computes the power and energy demand; energy generation; storage; distribution, monitoring and control.
The governance structure assigned specific roles and permissions to manage modifications effectively within the unified model.

It is worth noting that we did not conduct a comparative study of the presented approach versus a traditional one because of budget constraints and the burden of having two different teams working with different approaches.

RQ1: General nanosatellite mission modeling is shown through SysML stereotypes, requirement diagrams, trace/refine/derive/satisfy links, and model packages starting from customer needs and mission statements.
EPS is within the named low-level subsystem scope and EPS.# identifiers are described, but no EPS behavior, parametric model, or verification case is shown.

Limited early knowledge is handled through TBC statuses, iterative Phase-A/B refinement, and separating mission/system/subsystem requirement levels rather than through an EPS-specific minimal-behavior method.
RQ2: Reliability/quality, model reuse, traceability, and integrability benefits are claimed for MBSE/MDE and ADCS onboard-software development, not for EPS modeling.

RQ3: No EPS verification procedure is integrated into an EPS model in the paper.
The closest analogue is ADCS: a SysML parametric model calls MATLAB/Simulink, receives results, and automatically updates ADCS-F.34 requirement status before physical development.
